articles.content: STARBASE, Texas—Starship lifted off right on schedule Friday from South Texas, making its 15th test flight in more than three years. The largely successful launch took place in the early evening; as the massive rocket rose into the atmosphere, the Sun sank toward the western horizon. Conditions were ideal for the launch, with the atmospheric winds so calm the rocket’s white plume did not dissipate for many minutes. The weather in South Texas is not always comfortable; summers are long and hot. Friday evening was perfect at Starbase. The first stage ascended toward space flawlessly, releasing the upper stage above the Gulf of Mexico. From there, the Starship upper stage ignited its Raptor engines and powered its way into a nominal orbit. This was the second time SpaceX has flown Starship into low-Earth orbit. Read full article Comments

articles.content: Wildfires occur worldwide, and they can sometimes become serious threats to people's lives. A series of massive bushfires from 2019 to 2020 swept across southeastern Australia and destroyed thousands of homes. Recently, the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires spread widely across the city, resulting in massive damage to local communities. Many things can cause wildfires, but humans are the only factor that can also make preventative efforts. Measuring people's impact on fire is difficult because of the mix of human and natural influences. A team led by Jianghao Wang, a professor at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, recently published a study in Cell Reports Sustainability comparing the COVID-19 era with other years. Data from the 2020 lockdowns suggest that lower human activity at this time had the net effect of lowering average fire activity. Read full article Comments

articles.headline: ClickFix scam tricks users into infecting their own computers
articles.summary: A new 'ClickFix' scam tricks users into infecting their computers by mimicking familiar Captcha tests. Instead of image selection, victims are asked to press keyboard shortcuts like Windows Key + R and Ctrl + V, which pastes malicious code onto their system. According to Malwarebytes researcher Chris Fistonich, this is currently the most popular method for malware installation. The scam exploits users' trust in security software and their tendency to act quickly without thinking, highlighting a new security loophole in online browsing.

articles.summary: Meta outlines how Facebook and Instagram accounts are handled after a user's passing. articles.content: Beta Pictoris is a young star, roughly 20 million years old, and located about 64 light-years away from Earth. It is surrounded by a vast disk of dust and rubble where planets are still forming—astronomers have already found three. In a new Science study, a team led by Sarah Betti, an astronomer at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, used the James Webb Space Telescope to look for ice in this disk. Researchers found both water and carbon dioxide ice. The water ice is glassy rather than crystalline, and it is mixed with carbon dioxide in roughly the same proportions we see in comets of our own Solar System. This suggests ingredients necessary to form water-rich worlds might be common around young stars. The missing ice Beta Pictoris is one of the best studied stars in the sky. Its disk was among the first ever imaged, back in 1984, and we see it almost exactly edge-on, which makes it a natural laboratory for studying how planetary systems grow. It's what astronomers call a debris disk, where the dust is constantly replenished by collisions among comets and planetesimals, small bodies that are the building blocks of planets. articles.content: GLP-1 medications are everywhere these days. The peptide-based drugs are both highly effective and wildly popular for diabetes, weight loss and a growing range of connected chronic health conditions, including cardiovascular disease and obstructive sleep apnea. But, amid the boom, the latest data suggests millions of Americans have turned to unapproved versions and are using the potent drugs in ways doctors never intended, raising questions about what that real-world use means for safety and efficacy. In a study published this week , researchers at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention broke down survey data of GLP-1 use collected between July and August of 2025. Based on responses from over 8,000 US adults, the researchers estimate that about one in 10 US adults (9.8 percent) used a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, aka GLP-1 medication, in 2025. That's around 27 million adults. The study was published in the CDC's Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. Among GLP-1 users, nearly half (44 percent) reported using their GLP-1 in a way that was different from how it was prescribed. Users skipped doses, delayed getting refills, and used smaller doses than prescribed, among other changes. More than half of the people modifying how they used the drug said the changes were because of cost or availability reasons. Cost and access barriers were most pronounced among younger GLP-1 users. Fifty-eight percent of adults 14­–39 years old who modified their use cited cost as a barrier, compared with just 20 percent of adults 65 or older who said the same. Read full article Comments

articles.content: Elephants live in some of the most complex and resilient societies in the animal kingdom. Individuals die or move away, calves grow up, and newcomers join, but the local communities as a whole usually hold together. Long-term studies of African savanna elephants have shown that, even after poaching or other spikes in deaths, survivors tend to rebuild their lost connections over time. But a new study suggests that resilience may not keep the community intact when steady losses accumulate over time. Anastasia Madsen, a behavioral ecologist at the University of California, San Diego, and her colleagues analyzed 12 years of observations of wild Asian elephants in Sri Lanka. They found that, once losses began to outpace newcomers, the elephants’ society didn’t just get smaller. It fractured. Accidental savanna Udawalawe National Park in southern Sri Lanka was created in the 1970s around a reservoir on one of the country's four major rivers. “Before that, it was basically a tropical deciduous forest,” said Shermin de Silva, an ecologist at UC San Diego and senior author of the study (de Silva started the Udawalawe Elephant Research Project in 2006). Read full article Comments

articles.headline: Asian elephant societies fracture after steady losses outpace newcomers
articles.summary: A 12-year study of wild Asian elephants in Sri Lanka found that once deaths began to outpace new members joining, the social structure fractured rather than simply shrinking. Researchers from UC San Diego observed that steady accumulation of losses, rather than isolated events, disrupts the resilience of these complex societies. The findings highlight a critical threshold beyond which elephant communities cannot recover their social bonds.

articles.content: How do you think you're going to die? If you go by the current statistics for deaths in the US , it's reasonable to expect that cancer or heart disease will eventually get you. But OpenAI Foundation board member and Alignment Research Center Executive Director Paul Cristiano thinks we should all be worried about another major mortality risk. Speaking at a lecture series this week , Cristiano bluntly told the audience in a Toronto Convention Center, "I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident." In the opening lecture of a three-part series , Cristiano outlined his worries about the risk of an impending "AI takeover." He defined that as a situation where goal-pursuing AI systems "call the shots in the same sense that humans today call the shots and what happens on Earth" and where any human trying to stop them "would be as ineffective as if you or me was trying to stop the US military." Such a situation would likely lead to mass death and perhaps uninhabitable environments for humans, Cristiano said. Read full article Comments

articles.content: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day. On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System , which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System. Turning a Windows defense against itself The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions. The exploit uses Windows Defender to open a log file created by a standard user by calling ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature, a legitimate Defender function for processing antivirus signature updates. Read full article Comments

articles.headline: Meituan releases 1.6-trillion-parameter LongCat-2.5 model trained on Chinese hardware
articles.summary: Meituan has released the weights for LongCat-2.5, a 1.6-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model trained entirely on Chinese AI chips. The model activates 48 billion parameters per token and handles up to one million tokens via API. It achieves 88.4 points on Terminal Bench v2.1, approaching top Western models on coding tasks. The model supports text, images, and video, with 4-bit quantization for Chinese chip efficiency. Weights are available under MIT license via API and chat interface.

articles.content: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.” Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy. When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.” But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the company could implement them. “They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public. Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations. In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations. In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling. Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization. In early October, when lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in smuggling, MIT Technology Review asked the company if Fleet Intelligence could be used to prevent the practice. It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.” The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling. Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China. A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia. Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers. The Chip Security Act as drafted would require a mechanism to track the locations of chips, either by inspections of facilities, attestations by companies, or ping-based location mechanisms. The ping-based technique, the hardest option to circumvent, would require the GPU to send a signal of its location when it comes online. In September, the Center for Security and Emerging Technology found it would be the most cost-effective option. Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so. But if the requirements of the bill pass as part of the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, the new tracking mechanisms would only tell investigators where the chips are, not offer a way to disconnect them if it’s revealed they have been smuggled. Foster told MIT Technology Review he intends to introduce new, stricter legislation in the new year that would offer a workaround. The new rule would require licenses to operate advanced GPUs, and before a GPU could connect, its valid license would need to be verified. In the meantime, the controversy at Nvidia, Foster says, has fueled support among his colleagues for the rules in the bill: “There will be a lot of political pressure, in the wake of everything that’s happened, on the companies to actually do a very good job of the geographic validation of where the chip actually is.”

articles.content: The theme of day two of the AI Engineer Code Summit in San Francisco was increasing ambition using AI . And there have been few projects as ambitious as ArtCraft in the AI era. So far the fledgling company has released 17 open source versions of popular software tools , starting with a Photoshop alternative built from scratch in Rust called PhotoCraft . You could feel the excitement in the room this morning when ArtCraft founder and CEO Brandon Thomas presented a kind of manifesto for AI-based open source at AIE Code. When he mentioned that ArtCraft had cloned Adobe’s Acrobat, with a product called PdfCraft, it got a round of applause from the audience. In wrapping up, his rallying cries of “let's take back the entire internet” and “let's rebuild everything” were greeted with whoops and cheers. Thomas began his presentation by reliving the internet’s early history. In his view, the web started out with the right intentions, but things got screwed up once Web 2.0 hit the mainstream. “We had a bunch of chat applications that were completely open,” he said, regarding the 1990s internet. “So, IRC is like Discord, but you can spin up your own servers that you actually own. You can use whatever programs to automate them and interrogate them without rules.” His point wasn’t necessarily that everything was open source, but that web users could freely build things. With Flash, for example — a commercial animation tool eventually acquired by Adobe — “kids were making all kinds of animations.” When Web 2.0 came along, with its superior broadband and smartphones, “it brought everybody into the fold.” Thomas acknowledged that this widened the scope of internet software, but at the cost of that freedom to build with leading apps. “The diffuse, experimental, early web started to disappear,” he said. “The APIs got taken away from us, and then we started seeing distribution being gatekept by the big providers.” It seems Adobe in particular annoyed Thomas. He described getting billed with an unexpected fee when he cancelled a monthly plan. “It's really frustrating that the web — that was once really, really promising and open and free — has turned into this extractive, owned, rent-seeking world.” This inspired him to start ArtCraft, “with the ethos of ‘let's build everything open source.’” A message even anti-AI people have gotten behind, according to Thomas. In addition to PhotoCraft, they’ve copied other apps in the Adobe suite, cloned Figma, and created a Microsoft-like word processor called WordCraft. There are also independent apps such as SolidCraft, a community-led CAD project distributed through ArtCraft’s launcher. Thomas reiterated that these AI-built applications are 100% open — “not only the desktop apps, but the actual infrastructure as well.” PhotoCraft: The development process ArtCraft is starting with rewriting familiar tools. Thomas’s longer-term vision is for users (such as artists who were previously using Photoshop) to tailor the software to their own workflows. As he framed it, they want to “undo what had happened during Web 2.0 , when everything became owned and consolidated and gatekept, and just give people back their applications.” AI is the means to achieve that, he said. But aren’t there already open source alternatives to Photoshop, like GIMP? “GIMP isn't really used by artists,” said Thomas during his presentation. “We actually observed artists vibe coding their own workflows on top of the software that we gave them.” To begin creating PhotoCraft, the team gave an AI model a detailed prompt outlining Photoshop’s tools, data structures and file importers. After that, they “laid out a large, large prompt to say, let's build out the application.” As part of that process, they made everything MCP and CLI compatible . Within 24 hours, said Thomas, “we were looking at a pretty good approximation of what Photoshop was — and it kind of blew our minds away.” Thomas noted that PhotoCraft is “still not at 100% parity” — he said they’ve just passed 60% — but the team has set an internal goal to reach as close to 100% as possible. ( The project’s GitHub claims about 76% parity for feature breadth and about 46% for professional readiness.) “Right now, we want to fill the muscle memory of all the artists that use Adobe. So we are going for Adobe , their interface and ‘look and feel’ directly.” But after ArtCraft has achieved that, they plan to “build new apps that have new interfaces that are more agentic. ” A big reaction Thomas said he was surprised by the amount of attention PhotoCraft, in particular, has gotten — ranging from the New York Times requesting an interview, to a swelling of its open source community to about 4,000 developers . “I'm still struggling to bear with what has happened. It struck a nerve with people. They felt sort of maligned by Adobe and other tech companies . And what we built has really resonated with them.” ArtCraft’s apps are being downloaded at the rate of about 1.7 million per day, which Thomas said is still accelerating. In addition to the 17 official apps, there are around 300 being developed by the community, he added. Rust is key, but there have been technical challenges Other than the AI technology, Thomas said that Rust was a crucial part of making the apps performant — he claimed that PhotoCraft opens ten times faster than Photoshop, for example. “Rust was probably essential in this product's success,” he said. “We've seen people do it in Electron before, but for high-quality creative apps, you really need something that's native. ” For those engineers who are not experts in Rust, Thomas has good news for you. “Do you need to know Rust to start using Rust today as an engineer? Definitely not. [...] Your agents will drive it just fine.” However, Thomas admitted that not everything has gone swimmingly. “We've run into a lot of gotchas — like permissions, GitHub, scaling, CI,” he said. “CI is falling over.

articles.content: Today was the “System One day” of the second annual AIE CODE event , and somehow everything aligned: Cloudflare’s Michelle Chen walked through their Clef and Clairic models Richard covered Diogo’s triumphant return to AIE talking about the Jevolution with their most notable production customers since crossing $100M ARR In a BIG surprise, Google beat Anthropic to launching a production decision model, with Sundar and Logan announcing Gemini Decision 1 , a calibrated multimodal decision model capable of taking up to 1000 questions and costing $0.10 per million input with ~200ms e2e latency. Benchmarks are good ( usual caveat about benchmarks ): And you can hear all this and more on today’s System One track. And support AINews by giving your agent SerpApi to read and crawl the web! Sponsored by SerpApi Give Your AI Agents the Full Page, Not Just the Link Retrieve public web pages by URL as clean Markdown, structured JSON, or raw HTML with SerpApi’s Extract API . Extract a single page, map a site’s URLs, or run a bounded same-site crawl. Simply set engine=extract with a URL, and add output=md for Markdown. Pair it with 100+ SerpApi search APIs to go from query to page content with one provider. Thanks to SerpApi for working with business@latent.space! AI Twitter Recap Google Launches Gemini Decision 1 for Single-Pass Classification Gemini Decisions API : Google introduced a new API backed by Gemini Decision 1 . The model handles closed-set decisions, so it scores choices in a single pass instead of generating text token by token ( Sundar Pichai , Logan Kilpatrick , Google ). Specs : It supports yes/no, multiple-choice and rubric scoring, with up to 255 multiple-choice options. It accepts text, image, audio, video and PDF inputs, handles up to 1,000 questions per request, has 256K context, returns answers in 150–250 ms end to end, and attaches a confidence score to every answer ( @_philschmid ). Pricing : $0.10 per 1M input tokens, with $0 billed for output. Google says that is about 5x cheaper than Flash-Lite ( Sundar ). Origin : The project started as an internal Google DeepMind prototype. A small team shipped the model and API about six weeks later ( @_philschmid ). Google's comparison with TypeSafe's Jev : Google's own tests show Decision 1 beating Jev 1.14 on 5 of 7 shared benchmarks, including 92.2% vs 90.0% on JevBench. Jev costs $0.042 per 1M input tokens ( @kimmonismus ). Artificial Analysis evaluation : Independent results are more mixed ( Artificial Analysis ). Overall score : Decision 1 scores 66 on the Decision Index. That ties Elephant 9B and Jev 1.14, and sits 7 points behind Drex Max v1.1 and GLiDE v1.2. Strengths and weaknesses : It leads AA-Omniscience-Decision (66) and HLE-MultiChoice (49). On AA-Paperclip, it answers every question correctly on only 33% of documents, versus 63% for Drex Max. Cost and latency : It costs $345 per 1M tasks, versus $103 for Drex Max and $156 for Jev. Its Brier score is 0.18. Average time per task is 211 ms, slower than Jev at 92 ms ( latency ). Early adopters : Stitch built a rapid-design experiment on the API that goes from a rough prompt to a multi-screen product flow in about 5 seconds ( Stitch ). LangChain shipped day-zero support with a base class shared with TypeSafe classifiers ( LangChain ). Architecture pattern : At AI Engineer, Cloudflare described a hybrid agent design. Fast decision models handle tool selection and log extraction, and a large reasoning model handles diagnosis only. In its demo, this cut six LLM calls to one and about 40K tokens to 1.8K ( TheTuringPost ). Frontier Model Evals: Fable 5.2 Leads, Carbon Draws Speed Complaints Claude Fable 5.2 on Agent Arena : Fable 5.2 (Max) ranks #1 with a +30.4% net improvement across 4.7K real agentic sessions. That is about 1.6x the score of #2, Opus 5.5 (+19.5%). It is also #1 in Code, Work and Chat ( Arena , Pareto view ). Pricing : API prices drop from $10/$50 to $8/$40 per 1M input/output tokens. Median cost per task is $7.3, versus $5.5 for Opus 5.5, $1.5 for Gemini 4 Carbon (High) and $6.0 for GPT-6-Astra. Other evals : AA-Robotics v0.1 : Fable 5.2 leads at 75, ahead of Astra (69) and Sol (65) ( AA ). VIALS-AA (visual reasoning) : It scores 67% with tools but only 44% without them. Haiku 5.5 with tools reaches 49% at $0.07 per task ( AA ). Debate benchmark : It won 209 of 224 debates in a Cambridge Union-style contest ( @SamuelFitouss10 ). Effort calibration : Within the Claude lineup, Artificial Analysis finds that moving up a model tier beats raising effort: Opus 5.5 at xhigh outscores Sonnet 5.5 at max with 40% lower cost per task ( AA ). Vals separately reports that Fable's "high" setting is often cheaper and better than xhigh or max ( @RayanKrishnan ). Gemini 4 Carbon : Vals ranks Carbon #3 on its index, and the fastest and cheapest of the top five ( Vals ). Practitioner opinions conflict ( Theo , Martin Casado , @MParakhin ). Latency complaints : Theo measured Carbon at low effort taking 22m21s, versus 9m33s for Opus 5.5 at high ( timing ). He also reports about 11 seconds to first token, roughly 20x Fable's, and attributes the delay to the server side ( TTFT ). Coding and math : Casado calls Carbon "really good at code." Parakhin says Carbon often beats Fable on math and ML problems but that he does not trust it with coding. Muse Ember : Meta's model posts +1.7% on Agent Arena at about $0.02 per task. That is roughly 4x cheaper than GPT-6 Luna and Haiku 5.5, and about 12x faster than Luna ( Arena ). Vals reports Ember reaches 85% of Fable 5.2's performance at 0.84% of the cost ( Vals ). Chinese models : Qwen 4 : Qwen-4-Max appears to be live.

articles.content: As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape. Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ. It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words. But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid. One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables). The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport . Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity. Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out. Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand. The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company. Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid. But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out). The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale. Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency). Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do . But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation? Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers. Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think). Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that. But as one developer recently told me, industry insiders see their ambitions as constrained less by public opposition than by a lack of electricity. That should tell us something. So what happens next?

articles.title: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
articles.headline: Data center backlash driven by electricity demand, not culture war
articles.summary: Big Tech faces backlash over data centers as electricity demand, not cultural concerns, becomes the primary issue. articles.content: Today at the AI Engineer Code Summit , the main theme was system one models — non-generative models that return structured choices, scores, or probabilities. They’re also typically much faster and cheaper than reasoning LLMs (a.k.a. system two models). And who better to give an inspirational rallying cry for system one models than Diogo Almeida , co-founder and CEO of TypeSafe AI . Almeida was lead creator of Jev , the product that kicked off this trend less than two months ago. Jev was an instant revelation for AI engineers when it was released in September. In a podcast with Latent Space on launch (which quickly became our most popular episode of the year), Almeida explained the core problem with making LLMs the heart of software: reliability . In his keynote at AIE Code today, he took it a step further by claiming that Jev is “reliable intelligence” that should be used for “just automating everything.” Integrating system one models into code Of particular interest to AI engineers is Almeida’s point that system one models should become integrated with code. As he put it in his keynote, “code is the language of automation , therefore you need to integrate with code.” Latent Space founder swyx interprets this as a call to “liberally sprinkle ‘System One’ model calls everywhere INSIDE application code to make smarter software instead of increasingly convoluted forms of ‘concat strings together and hope for the best" AI engineering.’” The term “smart software” was used throughout Almeida’s presentation. It sounds like the kind of term used by companies like Microsoft or IBM during Web 2.0, but in the AI era it does actually signify a harsh reality about LLM-driven software: sometimes it’s just not very smart. As Almeida quipped during his presentation, “you get Einstein 95% of the time, but Mr. Bean 5% of the time.” “And if you can't tell which is which, how the fuck are you going to automate anything,” he added. Almeida ended with an impassioned plea to “automate everything.” Like an AI-pilled, pink-haired Steve Jobs, he called out to “the dreamers and the people who don't want to be limited by everything that has happened so far,” promising that TypeSafe AI wants to “really fight for you, and we want this to be as reliable as a fourth logic gate. ” How Glean uses Jev With the unenviable task of immediately following Almeida on stage, Chinmay Goyal from Glean presented a more prosaic version of Jev usage. He explained that system one models are used at Glean alongside LLMs and other types of classifiers, and that Jev is especially suited for “zero-shot flexibility.” “As the taxonomy of the decision space changes, we don't have to fine-tune these models again and again,” he said. In a short interview after his presentation, Goyal told Latent Space that their customers don’t actually need to know which type of model they’re using. “Jev powers a significant number of flows [but] the user just needs to have a product that works; that is always our aim with building anything. So we want to hide away all the complexity of whether we are using Jev or we are using a full-blown LLM.” In the conclusion of his presentation, Goyal offered some rules on when to use Jev: Jev patterns and prototypes Next up at AIE Code were Chibi Vikram and Kevin Bernstein from UiPath , a business orchestration and automation platform. One of their examples showed a test of Jev ranking document chunks . They held a “tournament” where Jev picked the most relevant chunks from small groups, then the winners advanced to another round, and so on. This whole process took under a second , even with thousands of Jev calls. “We realized that Jev is a building block that we can adjust ,” said Vikram about this and other experiments, “and we have to find these new strategies where we will be able to apply this building block. It might look less intelligent on its own, but with these strategies and patterns, we can get more intelligent — with even the current Jev model that we have.” Scott Roberts , a Principal Engineer at Workday , finished the ‘system one’ session at AIE Code with some prototypes his team has run with Jev. In one, an interface starts to fill in a time-off card while the user is still typing. It was an interesting showcase of Almeida’s idea that a fast model call can change what the software itself does. Roberts described it as going “from predicting what you want to say to predicting what you want to do.” Like the early internet The biggest learning I took from the System One presentations today is that a model like Jev can open up surprising new ways to build software . I was sitting next to a conference attendee who heads up AI at his company. He told me that in his spare time, he used Jev to create a website that sorts and ranks news about fantasy football. But the final word has to go to Almeida, who likened the new opportunities opened up by system one models to the experimentation of the early internet. “I think that there's going to be an explosion of what software can do, and we will want people to be exploring those boundaries of software. Not necessarily because it's valuable, but because they can, because we have new frontiers to explore , and this is what the early internet was like.”

articles.content: As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy. I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk. The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control. “It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.” Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Wiener has already had real influence on AI policy. SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed. Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation. Wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic. That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry , but Wiener says that couldn’t be further from the truth. “Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Big Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big Tech.” Wiener says that if Congress forms a select committee on artificial intelligence—something that Democrats have discussed since September—he’d be eager to serve. And he’s enthusiastic about many of the policy ideas floating around Congress. “I think it’s really important to have a strong, empowered, nimble federal regulator,” he says, noting that Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Democrat from California, has proposed legislation to establish such a regulator. He also highlights the importance of whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements, and a kill switch requirement, and he wants to see Congress leverage its oversight powers to hold the AI labs to account. “This is about the future of humanity, and we want to make sure that the public has a say and that the public knows what’s going on,” he says. And as a longtime state legislator, he is opposed to broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some of the proposed federal legislation would require. “States are, as Brandeis says , laboratories,” he notes. “You want the states to be able to continue to be nimble in ways that Congress sometimes is not.” Above all, Wiener says, he wants Congress to pass policies with real teeth. “It’s critically important that when Congress acts, that we do so in a way that is truly meaningful and that meets the moment,” he says. That means taking seriously the possibility of AI catastrophe, something he discusses in the sort of language typically used by AI safety experts. “We’re in a moment that is very dangerous in terms of the risk of loss of control over AI,” he told me. “We need to deal with recursive self-improvement. Once you’re in that realm, that really is potentially a recipe for total loss of control.” He’ll have some allies in the fight against catastrophic AI risk. Senator Bernie Sanders, for instance, has met with many of the AI safety movement’s most influential figures and has spoken repeatedly about AI and existential risk. But there’s still a large gap between Wiener’s Bay Area, AGI-pilled perspective and the national mood on AI, which is anchored by opposition to data centers. The fact that voters approved 40 out of 41 anti-data-center ballot measures on Tuesday might seem to be a good sign for Wiener and others who support AI regulation, but Wiener says he sees this movement as far more tied to local concerns than to bigger questions about AI risk. “Peoople who are really opposed to where AI is going—this is an area where they can actually do something about it,” he says. “But the data center revolt—to me, I think it’s more so that people are upset that there could be something like this in their community, with all the impacts near people’s homes, driving up electric bills and using water. I think that’s the bigger issue for most people, from what I can tell.” Wiener describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI, given its poor track record on regulating the tech industry. He also has concerns about the ability to get legislation past President Donald Trump, who called concerns about catastrophic AI risk a “hoax” in September and has demonstrated a stark unwillingness to collaborate with China, something that Wiener sees as essential to preventing the worst consequences of AI. But he says Trump’s unpredictability provides some measure of hope, though it’s a fraught kind of hope. “So far what we’ve seen are some problematic things, but not complete disasters,” Wiener says. “I hope that it doesn’t take a disaster to spur the president into acting.

articles.content: Our usual bar for making a fundraise a title story these days is a decacorn ($10B) valuation. We missed Mercor’s $10B Series C last year when it had less than $500m in revenue, but knew we wouldn’t have to wait too long til the next round, since it crossed $1B in Feb and $2B in June , it has now hit $3B annualized, surviving hacks : View post on X ↗ The company reports 5 million experts, and their TAM: “In the United States alone, there are more than 800 distinct occupations, each containing workflows that models have yet to be evaluated against.” And also this notable stat we are tracking: We’re seeing the impact of AI investment in our business. We already spend 3x as much on inference as on employee salaries, and it pays for itself by making our team better at their jobs . If that ratio holds as AI spreads through the rest of the economy, it points to something closer to double-digit GDP growth over the next five years, nearly 3x the rate we’re used to. We have yet to do a Mercor pod (will work on it!) but to better understand a data vendor business, you can look at our recent deep dive with Handshake AI , one of their competitors: AI News for 11/09/2026-11/10/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! AI Twitter Recap Gemini 4 Carbon Launch: Rollout, Pricing and Claimed Results Launch : Google released Gemini 4 Carbon as its strongest model for long-horizon agentic work in software engineering, cybersecurity, knowledge work and science ( Google , Sundar Pichai ). Gemini 4 Argon remains Google's recommended default for most coding and knowledge work, with Carbon reserved for the hardest tasks ( Google AI ). Availability : Carbon is available through the Gemini API and AI Studio for paid developers, Android Studio and Gemini for business. Ultra subscribers can use it in the Gemini app, AI Mode and Antigravity. Scientists can apply for 6 months of free access, and cyber defenders can apply through the Fairwind program ( Google AI ). Same-day integrations shipped in Cursor, Devin, Perplexity and GitHub Copilot ( Copilot ). Pricing : In Cursor, Carbon costs $2/$10 per million input/output tokens through Nov 30, rising to $4/$20 on Dec 1 ( Cursor ). Developer notes : Upgrading from Argon only requires changing the model ID to gemini-4-carbon . Google cites long decode up to 1M tokens and recommends thinking_level medium for most tasks ( @_philschmid ). /swarm in Antigravity : A new slash command turns one prompt into a multi-agent team that coordinates on a live message board. Each role can use a different model, for example Carbon for architecture and auditing and Flash for parallel edits ( Antigravity ). Google's showcase demo is a pelican-on-a-bike 3D campus game, with subagents rigging assets in Blender ( Sundar Pichai ). Official and partner claims : Google internal results : +25% open-source vulnerability recall over Argon, and 40x more remote protein homologs found for AlphaFold 3 ( @_philschmid ). Coding benchmarks : Carbon tops CursorBench at 60.4% on high effort ( Cursor ). It scores 40.0% on FrontierCode 2.0, up from Argon's 26.3% ( Cognition ). Research agents : Perplexity reports 0.857 on WANDR at $5.86 per task, matching Fable 5.2 at 40% of the cost ( Perplexity ). Independent measurements : Vals Index : Carbon ranks #3, about 1pp behind Fable 5.2, at $10.51 vs $17.94 per test. It is #1 on Vals' Finance, Legal Research and Tax indices ( Vals ). ARC-AGI : ARC-AGI-3 scores are 99.1% ($4.6K) with the provider adapter and 65.1% ($7.2K) in the standard harness. ARC-AGI-2 is 94.2% at $0.38/task ( ARC Prize ). Vision : Roboflow ranks Carbon #1 overall, but last of 10 on both speed (81s per image) and cost ($91.89 per 1K images) ( @skalskip92 ). Agent Arena : Carbon's cost advantage over GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5 widens on the most expensive sessions ( Arena ). Caveats from testers : Early users report hallucinations, overconfidence and verbosity ( @krishnanrohit ). One tester found broken Undo and shifted export text after Carbon reported its checks as passing ( @kimmonismus ). Google's Logan Kilpatrick objected that Gemini was the only model not tested in its native harness on one comparison ( @OfficialLoganK ). Claude Fable 5.2 / Mythos 5.2: Evals, Token Cost and System Card Head-to-head evals : MKA : Fable 5.2 leads Google DeepMind's new Multimodal Knowledge Agent benchmark at 57% Climb WSR. Carbon scores 54% and Opus 5.5 53%. Cost per task is $31.97 for Fable vs $6.29 for Carbon and $1.11 for GPT-6.1 Sol. No model leads all 10 verticals ( Artificial Analysis ). VIALS-AA : Fable scores 67% on life-science visual reasoning, ahead of Carbon (64%) and GPT-6 Astra (63%). It averages about 37 tool calls per task, vs about 8 for Astra ( Artificial Analysis ). Labor and design : Fable reaches 41.3% on the Remote Labor Index, up from 17.9% for Fable 5.1 ( @kimmonismus ). It is #1 on 3D Design Arena with an Elo of 1540, priced at $8/$40 per million input/output tokens ( DesignArena ). RSI Index : Vals scores it 37.8, narrowly ahead of Opus 5.5 at 37.3 ( Vals ). Token efficiency : GDPx materials science : SemiAnalysis finds Fable costs 89% more than Astra and uses 4.3x more output tokens for roughly the same score. It costs 7.5x more than Carbon ( SemiAnalysis ). GDPx software engineering : Fable nearly triples Opus 5.5's score, but per-task cost rises by a similar multiple ( thread ). Domain strengths : Dylan Patel says Fable improves on chip design, SWE, biology and materials, but not on finance, legal or RSI.

articles.content: As companies look to accelerate innovation with artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced modeling, the primary challenge is connecting new technologies to reliable data, scientific expertise, and the practical realities of bringing products to market. For specialty chemicals manufacturer Lubrizol, digital transformation is all about giving researchers the tools to test ideas faster, make better-informed decisions, and develop more sustainable materials without compromising performance. Girish Rao, vice president of information technology at Lubrizol, says the company is building a digital foundation that connects business processes, modern data platforms, and cloud infrastructure to support its research and development (R&D) teams. Their goal is to combine decades of accumulated technical data with the deep expertise of chemists and engineers who understand customer needs as well as the physical constraints of their work. Data scientists can help identify patterns, test new hypotheses, and model possibilities before researchers conduct physical experiments. But, Rao emphasizes, “it’s not about replacing scientific judgment; it is about giving our scientists better tools.” Scientists, data scientists, and IT teams approach problems from different perspectives, prioritizing experimental validity, model performance, and platform security and scalability, respectively. By bringing these groups together in “fusion teams,” Lubrizol aligns them around shared objectives, starting with small pilots to build trust. “Once the trust is built between the team members and they know what value they’re about to create,” Rao says, “things go a lot better.” Cloud infrastructure also gives the company flexibility to access computing resources and modern tools without making the substantial investments required to build and maintain its own data centers. These capabilities could prove especially valuable in advancing sustainability. Digital modeling can help researchers evaluate more formulations, explore materials such as starch and corn-based alternatives, and assess trade-offs across a product’s life cycle. Promising a material in a laboratory is only the first step. Scaling production while meeting performance expectations, regulatory requirements, and financial constraints is still a tightrope walk, but AI’s ability to model multiple variables could help teams navigate those competing demands. Looking to the future, Rao expects AI, automation, advanced modeling, digital twins, and connected data to converge as laboratories become more intelligent and manufacturing plants more efficient. The opportunity, he suggests, lies in bringing these capabilities together responsibly and at scale. “It’s not just a single technology. I think it’s the combination of all of these, and it’ll be the ability to connect all these processes that are going to generate tremendous amounts of data.” This webcast is produced in partnership with Infosys. This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

articles.content: AI Engineer Code Summit kicked off today with a series of workshops, including from leading frontier labs OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind. I attended the OpenAI workshop, intriguingly titled “New Ways of Working with Codex” and hosted by two of its Developer Experience engineers, Dominik Kundel and Charlie Guo . The past year in coding agents has been one of constant product upgrades by all the frontier labs. But not all of these changes have gone smoothly. The shift to cloud , for example, is still confusing to many users of Codex, Claude and Antigravity. We’ve also seen new ways to work with agents. Personal agents like OpenAI’s dots and Anthropic’s Claude Duet can assist between sessions, while voice mode gives developers another way to steer coding tasks. OpenAI’s workshop addressed all three, and I also had some followup questions on these topics for Kundel, after the session. Guo began the workshop by listing a selection of things they’ve shipped in Codex since the AI Engineer World’s Fair in June 2026. “I had to cull this list in order to make it fit on the screen because there were too many things to put in here ,” he said. “I think the team has been shipping at an unbelievable rate.” The awkward transition to cloud Codex launched in May 2025 as “a cloud-based software engineering agent that can work on many tasks in parallel.” But Kundel admitted that “it took a while for models and harnesses to equalize into something where we can build a really engaging experience.” In other words, the cloud part of Codex has often been an awkward user experience. That began to change after DevDay in late-September, when a revamped version 2 of Codex Cloud was announced. Suddenly, cloud usage seemed more viable. As the DevDay announcement put it, you can “finally close your laptop now and your agents will keep working.” As explained in the official workshop writeup — hosted on ChatGPT Sites — the new version of Codex Cloud lets you “ publish an environment once and run multiple tasks in isolated instances of that setup.” “These can be shared within a company if you're working in a company, or you can just create your own,” said Kundel about these cloud environments . “You start off by picking the GitHub repositories that you want to have access to.” After the workshop, I admitted to Kundel that I still find Codex’s cloud functionality confusing — for instance, when I start a task locally and later want to move it to the cloud. “We definitely want to have it be easier,” Kundel replied. “Some of it is going to depend on managing the context differences . For example, yesterday what I ended up doing is I was working on something locally, and I just asked Codex to go and hand it off to the cloud.” That handoff to the cloud is something OpenAI is trying to improve for users. To demonstrate, Kundel reopened an existing cloud task in his browser and showed me that its Appshot, a local capture of a Mac app window, was still attached. Codex Cloud is now “just a background , like a different executor of where things are happening,” he continued. “And so in a similar vein, you can actually ask your local Codex to — for example — spin up a task on a cloud Codex. So they're all sort of merging together .” Voice as user interface One of the demos Kundel showed during the workshop was a new website for a fictional record company called Blossom Music. Kundel demonstrated live edits to the site and said he sometimes uses voice dictation when iterating this way . “You can really quickly iterate on these things and get to a world that you're actually envisioning with your stuff, especially if you're unsure what you actually want to get to,” he said. Later in the workshop, Guo explained that voice is an effective mode to use when delegating work to different agents . “Most people I see that use voice with coding essentially treat it as just a different medium on top of their normal work,” he said. But personally, he likes to use voice as a control plane , which he says allows him to control everything he’s doing in a code base. “I don't think about it [voice mode] as saying, here's the one lane of work that I'm doing right now with voice. I think about it as saying, how do I manage my threads? How do I check in on stuff? How do I pull data from other apps on the computer? How do I create new threads in the application? Just using my voice.” After the workshop, I asked Kundel what are some of the ways he is using voice in his work? He replied that dictation is one way he uses it, but another use case is to talk to his dot . “Since my dot has access to all of my dev boxes and my laptop and my cloud environments, it also has all the context on what I work on , what I do,” he told me. “And so I often talk to it on my way to work [...] to work through stuff, start up some PRs while I'm driving, so that when I come home or when I come to the office, I can go and review them. So, voice is incredibly powerful.” Dots Speaking of dots, personal agents were only briefly discussed in the workshop. Perhaps that’s because, as Guo admitted, they’re not entirely intuitive to developers. “As a Codex power user, dots feel a little bit awkward to work with,” he said. “I think because they're a new paradigm and because they're good at different things than the main Codex.” But he said there are three things he’s found useful for dots, as a power user.

articles.content: Today’s podcast comes from a real life mystery: We are big fans of Cloudflare’s developer platform, and Cloudflare Email is a convenient tool especially when all your domains are already on Cloudflare. So why do agents keep suggesting we use Resend despite having an existing “home bias” and much larger incumbent player? Well, we got the guy who “does AEO for resend” - the CEO of AEO, Zeno Rocha, who has been writing about AEO since 2024 and Agent Experience since Feb 2025 , on the pod today: In a recent AEO study, Claude Code picked Resend first in 64 of the 102 email recommendations the researchers could extract. SendGrid came first seven times, yet showed up 55 times as an alternative. If the developer asks an agent to implement email and accepts the patch, how often does anyone get around to trying the second choice? The study breaks down the results by model and app. Our more recent comprehensive AEO study was a bit more competitive, with Postmark coming up top for most models. Zeno Rocha, Resend’s co-founder and CEO, joined us to walk through what happens on both sides of that pull request. He says Resend had 4.3 million users and 120,000 paying customers when we recorded. He discovered one of them, Warner Bros. Discovery, by sorting through short .com domains in the customer database on a Saturday. The developer gets there before the model Resend’s first useful bit of distribution was an email template. While Zeno and his team were building the sending API, developers kept telling them how painful it was to get the email itself to look right. So they released React Email. You could build a template with it and send it through SendGrid. They even documented how. By the time a developer needed a different provider, some of Resend’s code was already in the repo. React Email Now try the same journey as an agent comparing providers. Resend’s pricing page has a slider. A person can drag it to the right volume and read off the price. Add .md to the URL and the agent gets a table it can read in one request. That’s the kind of change I liked in our Supabase interview too. You can ask whether a model has heard of your product. You can also open your own pricing table and see whether it can answer a customer’s question. 80 tools, or two? When we recorded, Resend’s MCP server had grown from roughly 20 tools or fewer at launch to more than 80. Zeno wants someone working in a chat client to be able to do what they can do in the dashboard. Sending an email gets the demo working. Inviting a teammate, checking usage and managing billing account for some of the long tail. The design looks especially interesting alongside Cloudflare’s Code Mode server , which exposes its API through two tools, search() and execute() . Zeno describes opening the collapsed tool calls in his own sessions to see what the agent actually did. In one, the result was too large to fit in context. Reducing the tool count wouldn’t by itself make that response any smaller. For someone designing an MCP server, that’s a cheap experiment worth borrowing: expand the result of a call you make every day and see how much of it the model actually needs. What happens after “send”? Getting an agent to pick the SDK still leaves the entire business of delivering the mail. Take click tracking. A provider can rewrite links through a shared tracking domain so it can count clicks. If one customer uses that domain for phishing and it gets blocklisted, links in another customer’s perfectly legitimate emails can suffer too. Zeno explains why Resend introduced custom tracking domains and why he wants to keep the free tier even though spammers can sign up for it. Custom tracking domains · Resend’s $3M safety commitment Watch the domain setup and pricing walkthroughs if you build developer tools. Stay for the last stretch if you know Zeno from Dracula. We get into what it’s like to build a company with a family and how much of a founder’s job comes down to finding a name that other people actually use. Show notes Zeno’s original Dracula announcement — the editor theme he launched in 2013. Zeno on what Claude Code chooses — his reading of the recommendation study and the differences between model versions. Resend’s MCP server — the integration behind the tool-count discussion. Anthropic on writing tools for agents — concrete approaches to returning less data when a tool result fills the context window. Resend’s anti-abuse handbook — what happens when a new sender signs up and where the team intervenes. Chapters 0:00 Cold open 0:59 From Dracula to email 5:02 When agents pick the API 6:54 Getting into the inbox 13:28 What tracking measures 17:05 Paying for trust 19:44 The DNS hurdle 23:55 React Email’s wedge 27:01 Measuring adoption 31:58 Owning the mail stack 37:55 Designing the MCP 46:29 CLI, SDKs and craft 52:41 Mail for agents 58:28 Writing for machines 1:06:00 Winning recommendations 1:12:14 Enterprise and pricing 1:16:51 Building with a family 1:23:26 Naming a category Resend - Zeno Rocha - Transcript.txt 94.65 KB • PLAIN File

articles.content: Editor’s note: With this post, we are launching a new series focused on trying new models and products with unbiased reviews. Reach out with suggestions to tips@latent.space. Naive-N0.5-Flash is a new open-weights model built for AI coding tasks and tuned to generate as many tokens per second as possible . It was developed by a Chinese company called NaiveAI , with the aim of speeding up engineering and research workflows so that teams can experiment, iterate and solve complex problems faster. The model is an evolution of Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.5 , which NaiveAI has trained further for long-context reasoning and paired with its own NaiveRT inference engine. Naive-N0.5-Flash arrives with a bold pitch: a model built largely by AI and trained to do AI research itself, with recursive self-improvement as the long-term goal. To see what changed, it helps to know where it started. MiMo-V2.5 is a 310B-parameter sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with 15B active parameters, trained on 48T tokens. Its language backbone inherits the hybrid design of MiMo-V2-Flash, which mixes sliding-window attention (SWA) with global self-attention. NaiveAI's recipe starts from those weights. Through continued, multi-stage training, the team adapted the checkpoint to DeepSeek Sparse Attention layers. According to the NaiveAI technical blog , this took roughly 3.25T additional tokens on top of MiMo's original 48T. About 3T of those additional tokens were trained at a fixed 1M context length and with a constant learning rate. Benchmarking NaiveAI vs. DeepSeek and Z.ai We benchmarked the ultrafast mode of Naive-N0.5-Flash against DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash , and then gave all three the same app-building prompts. The trade-off, we discovered, is that Naive-N0.5-Flash takes longer to reason through harder problems, yet it still delivers answers faster overall. However, that comes at a slightly higher cost per question — although that may be an acceptable price for applications where speed comes first. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash are two of the most popular models in OpenRouter . Both belong to the Flash model class and demonstrate excellent capabilities in AI-assisted coding . As of this writing, performance statistics for NaiveAI models are not yet available on Artificial Analysis . Therefore, we report the Intelligence Index scores of the models used in our comparison: Model Intelligence Index DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (Max): 45 GLM-5.3-Flash: 43 Naive-N0.5-Flash: not yet available Published benchmark results offer some insight into the new model's capabilities. They place its coding ability between the two comparison models, and ahead of both on NL2Repo-Bench . The table below shows benchmark scores reported in the official model cards and technical blog posts of the respective models. Sources: GLM-5.3-Flash – Technical Blog , DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 – Model Card , Naive AI – Research . Model NL2Repo-Bench DeepSWE v1.1 Agent's Last Exam (ALE) GLM-5.3-Flash 56.3 63.4 26.3 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 68.2 77.0 35.4 Naive-N0.5-Flash 71.9 67.8 32.4 Our own evaluations below look at the differences between these models in more detail. Speed and verbosity experiments Speed is the headline feature. 1 NaiveAI promises faster research iteration than comparable models, which matters to developers and AI researchers who need to test ideas quickly. 2 We evaluated each model on 10 randomly sampled, text-only questions at each of three difficulty levels: 10 easy questions from MATH-500 , 10 medium questions from GPQA-Diamond and 10 hard questions from HLE-Diamond . That makes 30 questions per model. All experiments used the same maximum completion-token limit of 256K. For each request, we recorded response speed (tokens per second, TPS), the total number of completion tokens, and end-to-end response time. The code for the experiments is at https://github.com/gbeltramo/llm-verbosity . The tables below report the mean and median across all 30 successful requests for each configuration. Throughput figures come from different sources: OpenRouter for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash, and server-side measurements for Naive-N0.5-Flash. They should be compared with that in mind. Key observations Naive-N0.5-Flash reports exceptionally high throughput , approaching or passing 1,000 tokens per second in both thinking configurations. Because its figures are server-side and the other models' figures come from OpenRouter, we do not claim an exact speed multiple over DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 or GLM 5.3 Flash. Thinking has a large effect on verbosity. On the hard HLE questions, Naive-N0.5-Flash with thinking on averaged about 108,500 completion tokens, roughly nine times the GLM 5.3 Flash (high) average and 11 times the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high) average. The medians tell a different story from the means. Across all 30 questions, the median completion for Naive-N0.5-Flash with thinking on was about 3,200 tokens, far below its average of more than 51,000. A small number of requests produced exceptionally long reasoning traces and pulled the average up. The same pattern appears, less sharply, in the other models. The tables also include end-to-end response time, which is the fairer basis for judging speed. The median question took 3.1 seconds with Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking), against 5.3 seconds for GLM 5.3 Flash (high) and 10.1 seconds for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high). The means are closer: 45.3 seconds for Naive-N0.5-Flash, 45.0 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, and 86.9 for GLM 5.3 Flash. On the hard questions, Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking) was slower on average than DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high) , at 89.8 seconds against 79.7. Two caveats apply. The sample is small, at 10 questions per difficulty level, and we did not grade answer accuracy. Short, fast replies are only useful if they are correct. App experiments We also asked the models to build the same web apps from the same initial prompt. We tested six combinations of model and thinking effort, with the thinking effort in parentheses: Naive-N0.5-Flash (no thinking) Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking) DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (low) DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high) GLM 5.3 Flash (low) GLM 5.3 Flash (high) The gallery of apps is available online.

articles.summary: NaiveAI released Naive-N0.5-Flash, an open-weights coding model built for maximum token throughput. articles.content: On Friday, we asked Jamin Ball what comes next for Anthropic’s IPO . On Monday the roadshow started and Anthropic shipped the long-anticipated next-version of Claude Fable and Mythos . Of course, it is the new top model in the world, taking back Opus 5.5’s #1 spot from Gemini 4 Carbon which had its brief moment in the sun (10 days). View post on X ↗ Fable comes with a 20% per token price cut… but is more token hungry, as both SemiAnalysis GDPx and Artificial Analysis agree: Fable 5.1 cost $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. Fable 5.2 costs $8 and $40 . Yet on GDPx, a benchmark of professional tasks, SemiAnalysis paid $88.15 per task, up from $67.16 . The run logs give a clue. Where Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 would try about 20 test cases, 5.2 sometimes wrote hundreds or thousands and spun up subagents to check its work independently. All that checking helped Fable take first place at 16.4% . You pay for the checks either way. Which effort setting should you put in production? On FrontierCode 2.0, Anthropic reports that Fable at High matched Opus 5.5 at Max for about half the cost per task… but don’t talk about Fable at Max. AI News for 11/07/2026-11/09/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! AI Twitter Recap Top Story: Claude Fable 5.2 / Mythos 5.2 Benchmarks, Economics, Restrictions, and First Impressions What happened Anthropic shipped Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, claiming both are "a step above Opus 5.5 in almost all the capabilities we evaluated." It tops most independent leaderboards. It also arrives with deliberate RSI nerfs, heavier per-task costs and restricted subscription access. Launch claims. @claudeai announced the pair as built for "the most daunting technical challenges," with gains in coding, reasoning and vision. @marktenenholtz flagged unusual system-card phrasing: "The model that underlies Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2." That implies a single shared base model. Vendor-reported headline numbers , per @kimmonismus : Up to 30% faster output than the 5.1 models. On FrontierCode 2.0, Fable 5.2 at High matched Opus 5.5 at Max for about half the cost per task, and at Xhigh it was the top released model. 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents formalized the existing proof of Fermat's Last Theorem in 30 hours. Opus 5.5 completed 26% in 18 hours on the same setup. Mythos 5.2 accurately modeled 28 of 34 gene-therapy capsids. Alignment was at or above recent Claude models, with external pre-release testing. Default effort. Medium is the default effort in the Claude apps and Claude Code. Pricing. $8/$40 per 1M input/output tokens, 20% below Fable 5.1's $10/$50 ( @jaminball , @arena ). The rest of the spec, per Artificial Analysis : Cache writes cost $10 (5-minute TTL) or $16 (1-hour TTL); cache reads cost $0.20. 1M-token context with text and image input. Five effort levels: low, medium, high, xhigh, max. Long-horizon demos from Anthropic. An OS was built from an empty folder by 1,000+ subagents over 8 days. It boots on a laptop and has its own kernel, disk/keyboard/network drivers, persistent storage, windowing, login, an installer and built-in Claude ( @kimmonismus ). Fable designed three working electronic devices from a short prompt ( @kimmonismus ). It proposed untested chemical synthesis routes. It improved on listed solutions to 72 open optimization problems. @RLanceMartin published the safety-bounded scaling write-up for the 1,000-agent FLT run. Subscription access. Ultra and Team Premium users get Fable "resets" scaled by tenure: 1 reset under 6 months, 2 for 6–12 months, 3 above 12 months, usable until March 8 ( @ClaudeDevs ; echoed by @bcherny and @edwinarbus ). Pro and Team Standard get a one-week trial capped at half the weekly limit, plus one reset. Fable can only consume 50% of a weekly limit. Data retention. Fable 5.2 requires data retention by default so Anthropic's safety classifiers can run. Zero data retention is available only to eligible enterprise customers ( @code ). Rollout, day one: Cursor ( @cursor_ai ). GitHub Copilot / VS Code, where it "solved more tasks than Fable 5.1 while using fewer steps and tool calls" ( @code ). Perplexity Computer (Pro/Max) and Search (Max) ( @perplexity_ai ). @AravSrinivas made it his "new default." Factory ( @factory ). Hermes Agent via Nous Portal and OpenRouter ( @Teknium ). Arena ( @arena ) and DesignArena ( @grx_xce ). Official model-selection guide. @ClaudeDevs published guidance on Fable vs Opus vs Sonnet vs Haiku. It covers when to raise effort instead of switching models, and when to push subagents to smaller models. Independent evals (facts) Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 ( @ArtificialAnlys , breakdown ): Fable 5.2 is #1 at 65 (max) . Fable 5.2 (max) — Index score 65 Gemini 4 Carbon (high) — Index score 60 Opus 5.5 (max) — Index score 59 GPT-6 Astra (max) — Index score 57 Fable 5.1 (max) — Index score 49 New records: HLE-Diamond — Fable 5.2 80% · Previous best 69% AA-Omniscience v1.1 — Fable 5.2 67 · Previous best 54 Terminal-Bench-Science — Fable 5.2 73% · Previous best 65% CritPt v2 hard — Fable 5.2 77% · Previous best 72% FrontierCode 2.0 — Fable 5.2 49% · Previous best 46% (Opus 5.5) Weaker spots: AA-Briefcase: 1785 Elo, within the confidence interval of Opus 5.5 (1800) and behind Sonnet 5.5 (1813). GDP.pdf: 24% all-pass vs 26% for Opus 5.5. Terminal-Bench 4.0: 60%, level with Opus 5.5 and behind Kimi K3.1 Pro (67%), Gemini 4 Carbon (65%) and Sonnet 5.5 (64%). AutomationBench-AA: 76%, ahead of Opus 5.5 (70%) but behind Gemini 4 Carbon (78%). Efficiency: At high and xhigh it scores 62 using about 98k output tokens per task, vs 173k for Opus 5.5 max.

articles.content: This is our first Latent Space deep dive with an AI data company . In roughly a year, Handshake’s AI training business went from launch to $1 billion in gross annualized revenue . What are frontier labs buying at that scale? What evals are models still nowhere close to human level on? Garrett Lord brought the people who build these reinforcement learning environments to show us. For the first time, we are walking through them live! To cover the scope of Handshake, we had to produce a very special joint podcast across our Science/Engineering/Research/Finance podcast hosts, because Handshake’s business runs across all these and more. Watch for three segments after the general intro: Finance. In the finance demo, the agent has to find its assignment in a bank’s email, work out which files govern the deal, and deliver a workbook. Watch what happens to one line in the client’s email about existing goodwill. The agent carries the number into Python and subtracts it. Collin points out that the model can explain the tax treatment when you ask it directly. The mistake comes when it has to recognize that this particular line of code is where the rule applies. Bio. Nick Magazine and Jonas Mueller show us VIALS, Handshake’s benchmark for interpreting the images scientists use at work. Nick puts nine slides of brain-tumor tissue on screen and asks which two show the most advanced vessel necrosis. Give yourself a moment before his answer. Nick picks H and I. The model picks those two and adds G. Watching Nick point to what’s missing from the tissue is more instructive than seeing the score. Coding. In a simulated file-access task, the team can inspect which files an agent read, whether it checked the copies, and what it did to the shell history afterward. A transcript of the agent’s final reply would miss most of what Steve Kelling and Nishant Ranka are evaluating.
