articles.content: The AI Engineer YouTube channel just crossed one million subscribers . Thank you to everyone who’s watched a talk, sent one to a teammate, or put something they learned into production. For this special, we wanted to sit down with someone who has to answer a question a lot of us are asking at work: what should a software engineer actually learn now? Mihail Eric has two places to test his answer. He teaches The Modern Software Developer at Stanford and leads AI at Monaco, where his colleagues use coding agents to ship software and investigate outages. I asked him to take us through the syllabus, then tell us which parts survived contact with his own engineering team. This is also meant as a preview for all of you joining us in San Francisco for AIE Code next week, as required knowledge for all the conversations with the speakers, sponsors and attendees you’re about to have. If you can see this as a LS subscriber and haven’t got a ticket yet, you can use this code for 30% off (no refunds, sorry) Last year’s homework takes one prompt The first run of CS146S had nine assignments and a capstone. In one exercise, students ran an AI code reviewer on a repo and evaluated its feedback. By the next run, Mihail figured students could one-shot a lot of those exercises. When he asked a room of Stanford sophomores and juniors how they coded, everyone he surveyed was already using an agent. So this time, part of the homework is contributing to an open-source project. The person who maintains the repo reviews the student’s patch. I like what that does to the assignment. You can ask an agent to implement a feature in an afternoon. You still have to find out whether the maintainer wants it, why the code behaves the way it does, and what else your patch might break. That conversation is also how a junior engineer gets to learn from a senior one. There’s an exercise in the episode you can borrow for your next PR. Geoffrey Litt’s explain-diff skill turns a change into a visual walkthrough, then quizzes you about it. Try it on a patch your agent just wrote. Which question do you have to reopen the code to answer? Watch the discussion . What Monaco buys, and what it builds At Monaco, the team evaluated code review products and kept using Devin. Agent workspaces went the other way. A background agent needs somewhere to run the product, reproduce a failure and test the patch. The details depend on how Monaco’s cloud is set up, so the team built its own workspaces. Mihail’s rule of thumb: “You buy to learn, and you build to keep.” One result is Hal. An engineer can ask it to investigate something that broke and open a PR. A salesperson can ask the same system how the product works. In one case the useful answer is a change someone can review. In the other, it’s an explanation you can give a customer. Give both people a wall of debugging output and you’ve only served one of them. The question I kept coming back to was what happens at the other end of the PR. An agent sees the current code. Where does it look to find out why the team rejected this same change six months ago? That takes us from Basis’s Authority Map to Mihail’s prediction that open-source repos will become agent-run software factories. It’s a good reason to send a student to a maintainer today. Someone still has to decide which change belongs in the project. If you’re building with coding agents, come join us at AI Engineer CODE . And if you’ve been teaching this stuff yourself, I’d love to hear which assignment you had to rewrite first. Show notes Stanford CS146S — The ten-week syllabus, assignments and open-source partners. You can also switch to the previous year’s course to compare. Build a coding agent and look inside Claude Code — Mihail’s walkthroughs of the tool loop and the harness around it. Understanding is the new bottleneck — Geoffrey Litt’s approach to learning what changed in an AI-written diff. Monaco’s agent-developer workspaces — The team’s reasoning for building a place where agents can run and test the app. How to Kill the Code Review and the underlying Faros study — Teams with high AI adoption merged 98% more PRs, while their PR review time was 91% longer. Basis’s Authority Map — Where an agent should look for current behavior, earlier decisions and intent. Stripe’s Minions — A production example of giving background coding agents an environment and a path to an engineer-reviewed PR. Boris Cherny’s Steps of AI Adoption — The five stages we pull up on screen near the end of the episode. Mihail on The Thinking Mode — EO Studio’s interview, excerpted at the start of ours. articles.content: 👋 Hey there, I’m Lenny. Each week, I share deeply researched product, growth, and career advice. For more: Lenny’s Jobs | Lenny’s Podcast | Lennybot | How I AI | Become an AI-Native Builder and my other favorite AI/PM courses . Subscribe now P.S. Get a full free year of Cursor, Notion, Replit, Lovable, Wispr Flow, Linear, ElevenLabs, PostHog, Granola, Brain.fm, Waking Up, and more, by becoming an Insider subscriber (while supplies last). Learn more . Welcome to my latest job market report, my second of 2026. Of the five reports I’ve done over the past few years, this one is the most surprising and interesting. Here’s what we’re seeing right now: PMs seem to be winning in the AI era Engineering demand has stalled Design is at a record low Everybody now needs to AI Tech jobs are concentrating in the Bay Area Remote is at a record low The tech job market is growing fast, but mostly outside of software (gasp!) This analysis is based on two proprietary datasets that I love working with: TrueUp , which powers Lenny’s Jobs and tracks global job openings at tech companies (over 9,000 companies). The second dataset comes from Live Data Technologies , which tracks job changes (hires, departures, and promotions) for 124 million professionals, and their hiring numbers below are specifically for the U.S. Looking at these together, we can triangulate common trends, and the differences between the datasets are themselves revealing. Thank you, Amit Taylor and Alex Hamilton , for sharing this amazing data with us. 🙏 Let’s get into it. P.S. If you’re looking for a job, check out Lenny’s Jobs ! Takeaway 1: Product managers seem to be benefiting most in the AI era There’s been a lot of talk about AI replacing product managers (“who needs ’em!”). But so far, the data is showing the exact opposite. There are more open PM roles than at any point in nearly four years, up 75% from the March 2023 low, and PM openings have grown faster than any other core tech role since the start of 2023 (+56%, compared with +43% for engineering). When we look at hiring numbers vs. just job openings, the story gets more interesting. Even though open roles are growing, actual hiring for every core product role has been flat or in decline over the past few years (see takeaway 7 for which roles are now growing fastest). But PM hiring has held up the best (by far). And PM is the only one of the five core roles whose share of hiring grew (from 16% in 2021 to 21% today). The fact that we’re seeing growth in PM openings (first set of charts) but a flat line and even a decline in hiring (second set of charts) tells me that there’s growing demand for PMs, but that landing great PMs is getting harder. Takeaway 2: Demand for engineers is plateauing For the first time in the history of this report, engineering job openings have stalled. Open engineering roles grew 29% through 2024, 15% through 2025, and just 2.5% this past year . There are fewer open eng roles at tech companies today than there were even this past March. The hiring data shows the same slowdown. Companies in the U.S. hired about 113,000 software engineers over the past 12 months (May 2025 to April 2026)—less than half the 2022 peak (239,000). And the number has dropped every year since 2022. Just like with PMs, engineering job openings are up while actual hiring is down (+44% vs. −17% since January 2024), so even as demand slows, landing great engineers is getting harder too. Two bright spots for engineers: One, demand for tech recruiters is on an absolute tear. We’re hitting record highs: open recruiter roles are up nearly 300% since mid-2023. This may be a leading indicator of a reacceleration of eng hiring, which we’ll be watching closely. Another bright spot is that in terms of absolute numbers, engineering is still the largest category of tech hiring, by far. Over 120,000 engineers were hired just in the U.S. in 2025. And there are still plenty of great engineering jobs out there. Over 65,000 to be exact . One additional new trend to watch within the engineering function is the rise of the forward deployed engineer (FDE) . FDE openings are exploding. Historically, there have been only a few dozen open FDE roles globally (mostly at Palantir), but openings started climbing in 2025 and are up 4.6x in the past year alone! There are currently around 1,500 open FDE roles . Note that this growth is likely a combination of increased demand for this job along with other job categories, like “sales engineer,” being rebranded as “FDE.” Either way, FDE is so hot right now. Also, a telling trend: security engineering is one of the fastest-growing specialties, right behind FDEs. On the flip side, demand for mobile and front-end engineers has been nearly halved in the past year. That’s wild. I think the story here is the collapse of specialized/siloed engineering disciplines, with smaller eng teams having broader ownership (thanks to AI). Takeaway 3: Demand for designers continues to hit record lows Unfortunately for my designer friends, design roles continue to decline. There are only about 1,900 open product design roles 1 at tech companies globally right now. Not that much higher than just open FDE roles. It’s the lowest we’ve seen since we started tracking, and down 28% from a year ago. 😥 Actual hiring data from Live Data Technologies tells the same story. U.S. companies hired about 12,600 product designers over the past 12 months, less than half as many as in 2022 (27,600), and the number has fallen every year since. Even more telling, the ratio of open PM roles to open design roles is trending further and further toward PM. There are now 3.8 open PM roles for every open design role.

articles.content: EvenLeads is a web app plus a Chrome extension. The web app finds public "looking to hire" posts and writes a draft reply. The extension posts that reply from the user's own account once they approve it, or on its own if they switch Auto-send on. Wiring the two together in Manifest V3 taught me a few things. 1. A content-script bridge between the dashboard and the extension The dashboard is an ordinary web page, so it can't call extension APIs. A small content script runs only on our own domain and relays messages: the page dispatches a CustomEvent with a request type and payload the content script picks it up and forwards it with chrome.runtime.sendMessage the background service worker handles it and answers the content script fires a response CustomEvent back to the page Every request type has a matching response type, so the page can time out cleanly when the extension isn't installed or was just reloaded. The whole thing is deliberately dull and easy to test. 2. Service workers die, so expect "Extension context invalidated" MV3 stops the background worker and starts it again whenever Chrome decides to. Anything held in memory disappears, and a page still talking to the old instance gets "Extension context invalidated". What helped: state lives in chrome.storage, never in module variables every message is handled as if it could be the first one after a restart the page detects an invalidated context and asks for a refresh instead of failing silently 3. Keep your own service worker logs You can't open DevTools on a user's service worker. The background script wraps console.log, warn and error and keeps the last 500 entries in a ring buffer. A test command over the same bridge returns that buffer, so when a send fails during testing I can read what the worker did without going near chrome://extensions. 4. The web app decides and the extension executes The extension never chooses what to send. It receives one task at a time, holds an in-flight lock so the same lead can't be sent twice, runs it and reports the result to the dashboard. Keeping decisions on the server keeps the extension small and much easier to reason about. 5. Intents instead of selectors LinkedIn, Reddit and Facebook change their markup often. Hard-coded selectors for the comment box or the send button would break constantly, so the extension uses a small declarative intent engine: open the composer, type, submit, verify. Each intent tries known selectors first and falls back to role and visible text. 6. Default to slow The extension could reply seconds after a post appears. By default it waits for a person. Instant replies to every matching post look automated however good the text is, and many communities don't allow vendor replies at all. Approval is the default and Auto-send is a switch the user turns on. Disclosure: an AI agent wrote this post from the EvenLeads code and posted it for me. I read and approved the text before it went up.

articles.content: Yeezy 350 V2 talk in 2026 usually says "they all sit under retail now". On GOAT that is only true for some sizes. A typical colorway costs about 37% less than retail in a size 4.5 and 40% more than retail in a size 12. I pulled per-size prices for 25 Yeezy Boost 350 V2 colorways from GOAT (US market, new in box) on November 15, 2026. That gave 585 size-level prices for sizes in stock. Here is what they show. 1. Every colorway has a size under retail, but the typical size is not All 25 colorways had at least one size with a lowest ask below the retail price. That is where the "Yeezys are dead" headline comes from: the product page shows the cheapest size. The middle-priced size tells a different story. For the typical colorway, the median size costs 32% more than retail. Only 8 of 25 colorways have their median size under retail: Colorway Retail Median size ask vs retail 'Carbon Beluga' $230 $196 -15% 'Salt' $230 $206 -10% 'Steel Grey' $230 $210 -9% 'Bone' $220 $204 -7% 'MX Rock' $230 $218 -5% The older, proven pairs still hold a real premium in a normal size: Colorway Retail Median size ask vs retail 'Beluga 2.0' $220 $525 +138% 'Black Reflective' $250 $535 +114% 'Oreo' $220 $405 +84% 'Bred' $220 $378 +72% 'Beluga' $220 $370 +68% 2. Small sizes are the cheap ones I compared each size's lowest ask to the shoe's retail price, then took the middle value across all 25 colorways. US men's size Median vs retail Colorways under retail in this size 4 -46% 21 of 25 4.5 -37% 20 of 24 5 -34% 22 of 25 5.5 -29% 20 of 25 6 -24% 18 of 25 6.5 to 7.5 -8% to +3% about half 8 to 10 +7% to +30% 8 to 12 of 25 10.5 to 12 +28% to +40% 2 to 4 of 25 12.5 to 15 +51% to +82% 0 to 3 This is the opposite of the Air Jordan 4, where I found the small sizes carry the biggest premium. A likely reason: the 350 V2 was restocked in big runs across the full size range, and the small sizes have the fewest buyers. If you wear a 4 to 6 (or buy for a teenager), the 350 is cheap in 2026. If you wear an 11 or bigger, you still pay well above the store price. Overall, 211 of the 585 size prices (36%) were below retail. 3. Asks sit right on the last sale Across sizes with both numbers, the median gap between the current lowest ask and the last sold price was 0.3%. 293 asks were above the last sale and 284 were at or below it. For in-stock sizes, the lowest ask is a fair guide to what the pair trades at. The extreme asks ($2,000+ on a size 3.5 or 15.5) are single sellers with no competition, not a market price. How to pull this yourself GOAT has no public price API and blocks plain requests. I built a tool on Apify that returns this data as a table: GOAT Sneaker Price Scraper . Input used for this article: { "queries" : [ "yeezy boost 350 v2" ] , "maxProductsPerInput" : 25 , "includeSizePrices" : true } Each product row has the retail price, release date, lowest ask, cheapest and most expensive size, premium vs retail, and a list of every size with its lowest ask, instant-ship ask, last sold price, and stock. Export to CSV, Excel, or JSON. This 25-product run with all sizes took 41 seconds. Cleaning I did: kept only sizes marked in stock with an ask, compared each size to its own colorway's retail price, and used medians so a single $2,000 listing does not move the result. Limits to know about Prices are US market, in US dollars. GOAT shows different prices to visitors from other countries. "New" means new shoes in a good box. Used pairs are a separate option. This is a one-day snapshot of the 25 colorways GOAT returned first for that search, not every 350 V2 ever made. Sizes 16 and 17 (+57% and +85%) are left out of the table to keep it short; sizes 3, 3.5 and 15.5 had only one to three colorways in stock. If a number looks wrong for a pair you know well, tell me and I will check it.

articles.content: Stardance, a global teen online hackathon hosted for teenagers by Hack Club, a nonprofit organization, had just recently ended. I had made many great projects, and I even got a 3D printer, completely for free, because of my work. I was locked and loaded to make another coding project, but I wasn't sure what program I should do it with. So, I stopped for a few days, and eventually found Pixl, something very like Stardance. In fact, they were so similar to each other that I was able to get right back into it and created Corpustein, a blazingly fast N-gram Markov Chain model with a configurable order and a rolling window system, in just 34 hours over 13 days. It is coded completely in the C++20 STL, and it provides an interactive and beautiful TUI just through a user-input loop and ANSI codes. If you are very confused as to what Corpustein is, it is a mini AI model that generates text token by token using a window of previous tokens (or words) and a container of all the possible n-grams (or groups of X tokens) based on the current window. This is what an N-gram Markov chain (plus a rolling window system) is. It also maintains a set of previously generated tokens to prevent repeating them, but allows common English words to be repeated. Corpustein is also the TUI that lets users interface with it. The thing that makes it different from what you probably think of when you hear "Artificial Intelligence" (most likely a Large Language Model) is that a Markov chain does not remember anything larger than its N-gram window, but an LLM has an attention model, which looks at a very long sequence of tokens to help generate responses. And, with LLMs, semantic similarity is automatically encoded as high-dimensional coordinates in a continuous vector space, while Markov Chains rely on matching exact word sequences. LLMs can also generate reasonable answers to questions they've never seen before because of how they learn more abstract rules, logic, and world knowledge. Whereas Markov Chains usually just repeat fragments of their training data. An LLM is also much slower than a Markov Chain and is way more resource-intensive. Think of Corpustein as a statistical or probabilistic model that generates mostly coherent English. In my previous project, MDEZ++, I didn't think I got enough experience with actual C++, without the Qt Framework simplifying everything for me. If you want to read the article about it, look here . I definitely can not say the same thing here. I think this was the best thing I've ever done for my low-level coding skills, ever. Check out the GitHub repository here . If you are a Hack Club member, you can access the project page here . If you want a quick download, check this table! Linux Windows macOS Linux Executable tar.gz (x86_64) Windows Executable ZIP (x86_64) Not Automatically Compiled by CI/CD Features Fast and Lightweight: Built only on the C++20 STL, Corpustein is fast and consumes virtually no resources. Custom Corpus Loading: Users can load custom corpus files to be used by Corpustein. Additionally, Corpustein comes with a vast array of default options already baked into the program for them to load. Automatic Configuration: Corpus files contain metadata that provides default settings for the model to use, determined by the content of the corpus by its creator. If the file appears to just be a normal text file without any sort of metadata, it will skip the default settings gracefully. Compatibility: With portable, native binaries automatically generated by the CI/CD for both Linux and Windows, Corpustein can be used on just about any system. Commands and Settings: Corpustein contains various commands users can run while in the interactive terminal environment to control many things about the model, like the order, maximum sentence count, and much more. Alternate Terminal Buffer: Corpustein uses an alternate terminal buffer to make a beautiful, stylized environment. Users are able to enable and disable this alternate terminal buffer right in the CLI. Discrete Handling: When the model runs out of token choices, instead of simply stopping the answer, it will choose a new, random token to continue generating text, with the user never knowing it ran out of tokens in the first place. Context-Intelligent Repetition Avoidance: Corpustein saves tokens to a history set to prevent repetition in its responses. It references tokens with a set of common English words to never force it into choosing a completely random token because of the avoidance of basic linguistic structural words Configurable Typewriting Animation: Instead of throwing the model's entire response to the terminal all at once because of how fast it is, it uses a configurable typewriting animation to make it more appealing. Devlogs 1: "Minimum Viable Product" For the past 5.5 hours, I have been working on Corpustein. Corpustein is a Markov Chain built in C++20. I don't have a nice description or branding phrase yet, because I have been waiting for it actually to be slightly usable. Before I make my README, I will set up a GitHub Actions workflow to automatically compile Linux AppImage and Windows EXE files and attach them to Releases. How it works is that the user inputs a prompt, like "What is a transistor?" and the first step is finding a token for the program to start its response with. If you are wondering, a token is one unit of text. Usually, it is a word (that is, for Corpustein), but it could also be a character, punctuation mark, sentence, etc. It will compare the tokens in the user's prompt to the corpus to find a word the user said that is also in the corpus. And basic words like "in", "there", "a", "an", etc., can never be the seed. If it can't find a good seed based on the input text, it will just do a random one.

articles.content: We introduced Kitesurf , our stateless browser for AI agents that runs entirely on top of Workers, in August and followed up in September with WebMCP support, new APIs, and improved compatibility. On every occasion, we mentioned our commitment to open sourcing it so that developers could run their own browser engine on their own Cloudflare accounts if they want to. That promise is now real. Kitesurf is open source on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. You can read the code, run it locally, change it, and deploy your own instance to Cloudflare Workers. A browser built for agents Kitesurf runs entirely on Cloudflare Workers. It parses HTML, applies CSS, executes page JavaScript, and renders screenshots without a browser container. It supports the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP), so you can connect clients such as Puppeteer. Our main goal is to give AI agents a lightweight, efficient browser — one that can load websites, execute JavaScript, and interact with pages while using less CPU and memory than a full browser like Chromium, and scaling on demand across Cloudflare’s global Workers network.

articles.content: The dashboard stopped updating. The ESP32 kept measuring temperatures. The Raspberry Pi was still running. So where did the readings go? I put together a small MQTT debugging scenario using four log files: ESP32 firmware log Raspberry Pi system journal Mosquitto broker log Dashboard application log The interesting part wasn't finding the disconnect message. It was reconstructing what happened before, during, and after the outage . By combining the logs into a single timeline, I could trace the broker shutdown, compare the clients' reconnection behavior, and identify four measurements that were taken but never published. I documented the investigation step by step, including screenshots and reusable highlighting tokens: I wish I’d had a tool like Emlyzer sooner. Here’s how I debug an MQTT outage with it. The temperature on my dashboard is stuck at 22.40 °C. The ESP32 is still taking readings. The Raspberry Pi is still on the network. And the dashboard has one clue: MQTT disconnected. That gives me a place to start. I want to know what broke first, what happened to the readings in between, and when the dashboard finally caught up. I start by following a single reading I open four logs in Emlyzer: the ESP32 firmware log, the Pi’s system journal, the Mosquitto log, and the dashboard log. To see how a temperature reading gets from the ESP32 to the dashboard, I select seq=1724 . The sequence number ties the firmware and dashboard entries together, and the Mosquitto entries in between show the broker receiving and forwarding a message on the temperature topic. There’s also a lab-health entry from journal.log among the surrounding lines. The dashboard warning gives me my first highlight token, disconnected . It also picks out MQTT_EVENT_DISCONNECTED on the ESP32, 45 milliseconds after the dashboard warning. I look just before those two entries in the Pi’s journal. Mosquitto was already stopping. I add tokens for Stopping mosquitto.service and Started mosquitto.service to mark the interruption. A different color for New client connected makes it easy to spot when each client comes back. The broker comes back before the readings do In dashboard.log , I find the last reading before the gap, seq=1841 . At 10:15:02.010 , systemd begins shutting down Mosquitto, and the dashboard and ESP32 lose their connections. Once the broker is back up, the dashboard subscribes again and the sensor reconnects. The first reading to reach the dashboard after the gap is seq=1846 . The Pi journal puts the client errors in order. The service was already stopping when the dashboard lost its connection, and both retry failures occurred before the service came back. The two clients then recovered on different schedules. The dashboard subscribed again almost two seconds before the sensor reconnected. The dashboard goes ten seconds between readings. Four measurements are missing. Where did they go? The firmware log shows that the ESP32 took readings 1842 through 1845 but skipped publishing them while its MQTT connection was unavailable. Then comes 1846 . I add seq=1846 as a token and follow it from the firmware queue at 10:15:10.020 to the dashboard 35 milliseconds later. Mosquitto logs a publish arriving and being forwarded on the temperature topic in between. The sequence number ties the two ends together, and the broker’s topic and timestamps show the handoff. The service journal shows the stop and subsequent start. In this demo the restart is intentional. In a field capture I’d look for the trigger in operator, deployment, or audit records before attributing the restart to a person or a job. The next outage starts with a saved token set Before closing the logs, I save the tokens I built during the investigation as MQTT Connection Issue.etk . When the dashboard freezes again, I can open the new logs and load that file. The searches and colors are already there. I can go straight to the service events, see which client reconnected first, and check whether readings resumed. A colleague investigating a similar issue can start with the same file. Some clues travel better than others. The service and connection tokens apply to another capture with the same log wording. The token seq=1846 belongs to this run. Next time I’d replace it with the sequence number I’m following. If a new failure turns up a useful search, such as reconnect failed , I can save it in the set for the next investigation. Want to investigate it yourself? I've made the example logs and token files available through the Emlyzer GitHub repository. I'm curious how others approach this: when debugging communication issues across embedded devices, brokers, and applications, do you usually inspect each log separately, or do you combine them into a common timeline? Originally published on emlyzer.com .

articles.title: Debugging an MQTT Outage Across ESP32, Raspberry Pi, and Mosquitto Logs
articles.headline: MQTT outage traced across ESP32, Raspberry Pi, and Mosquitto logs
articles.summary: A temperature dashboard stopped updating after an MQTT broker shutdown. By combining four log files into a timeline, the investigation found the broker stopped before the dashboard lost connection. The ESP32 took four readings (seq 1842-1845) that were never published due to the disconnected MQTT link. After the broker restarted, the dashboard reconnected 2 seconds before the sensor, and the first recovered reading (seq 1846) arrived 35 milliseconds later.

articles.content: AI agents can write the code, choose the packages, and run the install. Who’s checking what they just invited onto your machine? This week I’m joined by Ahmad Nassri, CTO of Socket and former CTO of npm. We get into the trust built into a package install, the new ways attackers are using agents, and what it takes to keep building without handing over the keys or your wallet. Join the discussion Changelog++ members get a bonus 6 minutes at the end of this episode and zero ads. Join today! Sponsors: WorkOS – WorkOS is building the infrastructure for the AI era. Explore three new product previews: Airlock for secure AI agent permissions, Atlas for deploying AI-built internal apps, and Passport for seamless, passwordless access to work apps. See the announcements, demos, and highlights in the WorkOS init() 2026 recap . Parallel – Web infrastructure for AI to search, extract, monitor, and reason over the world’s information. Deepgram – Speech-to-text, text-to-speech, and voice agent APIs for developers building voice AI applications. Fly.io – The home of Changelog.com — Computers for agents, from sandboxes to production. Give your agent its own hardware-isolated Linux computer. Deploy what it builds without changing platforms. Featuring: Ahmad Nassri – Website , GitHub , LinkedIn , X Adam Stacoviak – Website , GitHub , LinkedIn , Mastodon , X Show Notes: The Hidden Blast Radius of the Axios Compromise Socket Firewall npm trusted publishing Shai-Hulud Zero Day Clock Something missing or broken? PRs welcome!

articles.title: All your packages are belong to us
articles.headline: AI agents can install packages without human oversight
articles.summary: Ahmad Nassri, CTO of Socket and former CTO of npm, discusses how AI agents can autonomously write code, select packages, and execute installations. The conversation explores the trust inherent in package installs, new attack vectors using agents, and strategies to maintain security without surrendering control or financial access.

articles.content: We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability. The short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate. However, write outages, monitoring gaps during data migrations, and a regional network disruption reinforced the need for capacity growth to be paired with safer operations, stronger isolation, and validated regional recovery. As of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US. Azure served 63% of migrated-service reads, 66% of monolith reads, and 52% of Git reads. We also completed a compute expansion across all nine Central US Kubernetes clusters, more than doubling capacity. That capacity is already carrying real growth. Migrated-service traffic has increased 82% since March, with Central US absorbing the growth beyond the highest weekly-average load previously served from our existing datacenter. This gives GitHub more room to grow without pushing the original environment beyond its prior operating range. We also made several targeted reliability improvements. Actions changes increased capacity for critical Azure control-plane requests. A separate NAT-gateway mitigation reduced usage by 85%; four production jobs failed during the change, compared with approximately 800 expected without the mitigation. Connection limits and other client improvements now also reduce the chance that a dependency interruption becomes a broader reconnect storm. We removed concentrated sources of database load as well. A high-traffic GitHub Actions endpoint handling more than 250 million requests per day moved to a more efficient service path, reducing peak database reads by 85%. Requiring at least three characters before searching repository topics reduced slow or terminated queries for that pattern by approximately 98%. Reliability was still not where it needed to be. The October 7 write outages exposed an unsafe interaction between database orchestration and production routing. An October 29 Azure network disruption affected all three Central US availability zones and at least 34,128 signed-in users. More details on these and other incidents follow. The East US 3 buildout is about one week behind plan. The next phase starts with its first validated traffic ramp in the first week of December, while we continue hardening migration safety, dependency isolation, and regional recovery. The principle remains the same: availability, then capacity, then features. October 05 19:11 UTC (lasting 3 hours and 38 minutes) Duration: approximately 3 hours and 45 minutes. Customers may have seen GitHub Actions jobs on GitHub-hosted runners stay queued much longer than usual, and some workflow runs failed to start. During the worst stretch, which lasted about 90 minutes, most jobs on GitHub-hosted runners did not start within five minutes. Impact eased as we failed over to healthy regions and added capacity. Self-hosted runners were not affected. GitHub Pages sites that build with actions were slow to update, though existing sites continued to serve normally. Some customers also saw errors in repository lists, licensing and billing pages, and some Copilot features. What went wrong and why? Actions jobs stayed queued or failed to start because the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners stopped working reliably. A partial networking failure on our cloud provider’s side disrupted some of the connections between one of our datacenter regions and the cloud-hosted databases that service depends on. Instead of failing fast, the service waited for those calls to time out. The waiting calls piled up until the service ran out of memory and restarted. Jobs then shifted to the same service in a healthy region, which did not have enough capacity for the extra demand and began failing too. At the same time, runners that went several minutes without receiving a job shut down and were slow to be replaced, so fewer runners were available to pick up jobs. How did we respond? A partial networking failure began, and actions jobs started backing up. Alerts flagged errors and slow job assignment, and we declared an incident. We redeployed the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners, but it did not recover. We traced the failures to the networking issue. We failed over the affected databases and storage to healthy regions, one service at a time, and added capacity. Actions recovered, but some other affected services kept failing even after failover. We worked with our cloud provider to resolve the networking failure. The remaining services recovered, and we resolved the incident. How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful? We are making the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners better able to handle sudden increases in load, so it keeps up when another region shifts extra jobs to it. We now have expanded prioritization of runner assignment based on customer profile when available runner capacity is degraded. We are changing the behavior of GitHub-hosted runners to reduce recovery time when job assignment services are degraded for a period of time. We are improving how quickly we detect and locate partial network failures between our datacenters and the cloud-hosted services they depend on. October 06 19:57 UTC (lasting 3 hours and 43 minutes) Duration: approximately 6 minutes of failed or slow requests across github.com, followed by approximately 3 hours and 30 minutes during which enterprise migrations were paused. Customers may have seen server errors or slow responses when signing in, working with repositories and pull requests, calling the API, or using GitHub Codespaces. Retrying a short time later would have succeeded, and delayed webhook deliveries caught up soon after. At the peak, about 1.3% of all requests failed or timed out, and about 6.4K organizations saw at least one failed or slow request. Migrations were paused for customers using GitHub Enterprise Importer, and were resumed once a fix was deployed. What went wrong and why? A surge in migration activity caused GitHub Enterprise Importer to send a burst of very large queries to a shared database.

articles.title: GitHub availability report: October 2026

articles.content: Over the last month, the number of Large Language Model (LLM) penetration testing and orchestration frameworks has exploded. Just a few weeks ago, ARTEX — an open source agentic penetration testing system that automates offensive security workflows — was the only framework available. In just the last three days, we have seen over 50 framework families attempt to scan Cloudflare customers globally. The number of Internet Protocol (IP) addresses seen running these frameworks has grown into the thousands and continues to increase daily. The proliferation of these frameworks has significantly changed the status quo in cyber defense: defenders are struggling to keep up with the volumetric nature of these autonomously guided attacks. ARTEX was taken down by its creator Autumn-27 on October 8. (“The malicious exploitation of this tool runs entirely counter to its original intent,” they wrote in Chinese. ) But in the month since, the ecosystem has exploded with new fragmented versions of it. There are now over 12,000 repositories, with several hundred unique forks containing lineage from the original repository. Additionally, hundreds of other similar agentic orchestration frameworks have been created since October 8. Daily requests of AI penetration testing (pentesting) and exploitation tools has grown by 30x since October 1. These tools have also begun chaining stolen customer credentials in some of the more complex attacks, such as lateral movement chaining throughout an environment. We expect these frameworks to continue to proliferate, and every organization should be prepared to address this threat. To counter LLM-based pentest frameworks, we recommend that all organizations adopt what we call the Modern Security Model, which has six key pillars: Fortify the front gate : Implement a Web Application Firewall (WAF) with advanced rules such as rate limits. Security station in the foyer : Anomaly detection on all web applications your customers access. Identify phony visitors : Implement Bot Defense. Remove the back door : Implement Identity-Gated Access for all high-risk external and internal web applications. Inspect deliveries: Enforce validated schemas and explicit security controls. Neighborhood watch : Implement Threat Intelligence to gain visibility into attacks. What is an LLM penetration and exploitation orchestrator? Open-source pentesting frameworks are able to orchestrate AI agents to carry out stages of the traditional Cyber Kill Chain at scale. Tools like ARTEX have the ability to quickly plug in existing Model Context Protocol (MCP) and connect traditional standalone pentesting tools in novel ways. Some even allow operator direction on what type of task to accomplish. These tools can map and enumerate environments, both from the inside and outside. ARTEX and its forks map assets and environments onto a graph, allowing multiple independent parallel agents to enumerate, verify, prototype, and attack at the speed of inference. These tools turn compromises into a hill-climbable problem, which agents are specifically good at. The AI LLM pentesting tools that currently exist We are currently tracking 50+ AI LLM agents. The table below shows the top five LLM penetration and exploitation orchestrators. Each is extremely popular (1k+ GitHub stars) and fully autonomous. The fully autonomous nature of these agents represents a doctrinal shift in offensive cyber capabilities: Human skills are no longer the limit: A harness performs every step of the OODA loop by observing the environment, orienting itself to prioritize valuable and/or vulnerable targets, decide on an action, and act autonomously. Speed increase: Having multiple parallel agents working towards a goal is a large shift compared to single operator or multiple operator augmented by AI. Scale: A single operator can target multiple organizations at the same time, greatly increasing their blast radius. Small mistakes are easily discovered: Autonomous frameworks relentlessly and systematically test exposed services, including their configurations. Architecture Planning model Built-in capabilities/execution environment Post-exploitation capabilities ARTEX (and forks) Planner and parallel agents Graph of goals, leads, and findings is linked to separate asset graph of target Directly on host or container with network/root access, can install/develop tools as needed Nothing built-in, requires user instruction LuaN1aoAgent Supervisor agent, planner agent, and generic executor agents Three graphs, with goals/tasks/blockers, evidence/hypothesises/exploits, and target/local Container with network/user access, can develop tools as needed and install user packages Built-in SSH and Chisel for tunneling and attempted reconnection after disruption Decepticon Orchestrator agent dispatching specialist sub-agents Graph of objectives with prerequisites Kali container running as root, can develop tools as needed Dedicated post-access, Active Directory and cloud pivoting skills Cairn Dispatcher orchestrating work to existing AI harnesses (Codex, Claude Code, Pi) Graph of facts and leads; new nodes trigger dispatcher Kali container with root access or directly on host, can develop tools as needed Prompt guidance and Kali tools PentestGPT-Agent Supervisor agent and one generic executor agent Task list with dependencies, goals, and evidence Run on host, can develop tools as needed Nothing built-in, requires user instruction Observations from the world's largest network As of November 12, ARTEX and its forks make up over 60% of currently known AI penetration testing orchestrators. The charts below help us understand how adoption of these tools has changed over the past six weeks. Since the removal of the original ARTEX repository on October 8, traffic has grown more than tenfold, and has increased more than 30x since October 1. As demonstrated above, the takedown of ARTEX on October 8 (and widespread reporting of it) likely caused a hydra effect, where the removal of the original repository led to a massive increase in the number of forks and modifications which can be seen in the steep acceleration of unique instances around October 8. Identity-chained LLM exploitation Over the last eight weeks, our Cloudforce One team has been called into multiple incident response investigations involving ARTEX and ARTEX-derived LLM exploitation frameworks. We’ve seen firsthand how exposed credentials are being chained with LLM-based exploitation frameworks to gain the upper hand over defenders. We observed multiple incidents in which a threat actor gained initial access to a hyperscaler environment and pivoted directly into the customer's Cloudflare environment. Root-cause analysis revealed a common credential hygiene failure.

articles.title: Adapting to AI penetration testing orchestrators: The Modern Security Model
articles.headline: Cloudflare reports 30x surge in AI penetration testing tools since October 1
articles.summary: Cloudflare's Cloudforce One team observed over 50 AI penetration testing framework families scanning customers globally, with IP addresses running these tools growing into the thousands daily. Since the takedown of ARTEX on October 8, the ecosystem exploded with over 12,000 repositories and 30x increase in daily requests. The report details how these autonomous tools map environments, chain stolen credentials, and pivot across hyperscaler infrastructure, prompting Cloudflare to advocate for a Modern Security Model to defend against AI-driven offensive capabilities.

articles.content: You're wrapping up a demo video, a screen recording, a clip an agent just rendered. Then the boring part starts: the tool you want to feed it to doesn't want a file. It wants a URL. Some social publishing tools work this way. So do a lot of APIs, automation platforms, and agents. They accept a video URL, not an upload dialog. So you end up pushing the file to some random host, waiting for a transcode you didn't ask for, and getting back a watch page instead of a link to the actual video. I got tired of that last mile, so I built the thing I wanted: Video to URL , a free tool that does exactly one job. Drop an MP4, get a public, seekable link. A few things it deliberately does NOT do: No signup. The anonymous link works the moment the upload finishes. No transcoding. The file is stored and served as-is, byte for byte. No recompression, no quality loss, no waiting for a "processing" spinner. No watch page. You get a direct CDN URL you can paste into an API call, an HTML <video> tag, or any tool that takes a video URL. Standard players can seek through it, because the CDN answers HTTP range requests. The limits, up front: MP4 only, up to 25 MB on the anonymous tool, and anonymous links disappear within 24 hours. If you upload something and want to keep it, there's a "Keep this video" button right on the result: it saves that exact MP4 to a free account, no second upload. Bigger files (100 MB on Starter, 250 MB on Pro) and automated uploads go through the video upload API . That's the whole thing. A file goes in, a link comes out, and the person opening it never has to know PixelVault exists. If you try it and hit a wall, tell me in the comments - the tool exists because of walls I kept hitting myself.

articles.content: How many times this week did you re-explain the same task to an agent? How many times did you ask your colleague with deep institutional knowledge how to solve a specific problem? That context shouldn’t be lost in a chat or locked in one person’s head. Agent skills let you capture repeatable instructions so you and your agents can reuse them. The skill you write for yourself tonight can later become part of a team’s pipeline. An agent skill is a versioned directory centered on a SKILL.md file that describes when and how to do a repeatable task. You can share those instructions across agents, but the environment still needs to provide the tools, credentials, and permissions to carry them out. A skill can describe how to query a database, for example, but it doesn’t grant access to that database. I covered this topic live with Shishir Tewari, Senior Manager, Data Engineering at Procore, during GitHub Universe 2026. Our session was titled “Build once, run on any agent: a practical guide to agent skills” . Define one job and when it applies A skill works best when it has a clear job, input, and output. For example, let’s say you’re building an agent that checks AI-generated changes against the original request. If the same agent assesses its own work, its explanation might influence the review. With Proof Agent , we use a separate verifier to examine the changes and provide evidence for its findings. The skill’s frontmatter names the task and describes its purpose: --- name: proof-agent description: Adversarial verification of AI-generated work. Spawns an independent verifier to check for false claims, broken code, and security issues. --- At the center is a simple rule: self-verification is not verification. The When to Verify section in Proof Agent’s SKILL.md says when to invoke the skill. The remaining instructions explain what the verifier reviews and what evidence to include in its findings. Coordinate multiple skills for a larger workflow When the judgment that makes a data pipeline correct lives in four different people’s heads, those four people are the roadmap. Each change to the pipeline depends on their availability and knowledge of the data. Data Forge is an example of how to capture parts of that judgment in skills that work together. In the support-desk pipeline example , we start with a request for metrics that count incidents created and resolved. Before building the pipeline, the forge-init skill discovers details such as source tables and naming conventions, then writes them to a resolved manifest. The other skills read that manifest for the project context they need. The forge-builder skill then coordinates the work from the issue through to a pull request. It uses forge-dbx to query the data platform and forge-lint to apply the team’s standards as it designs and builds the pipeline. A person reviews the proposed decisions along the way, and the resulting pull request contains the pipeline code, schema changes, and tests. Each skill has a defined responsibility, and they share project context instead of rediscovering it independently. When a step changes, you can change one skill and leave the rest alone. Skills fit bounded, repeatable work that benefits from reusable judgment, such as a checklist, release, migration, or metric pipeline. If a workflow needs a stable interface, shared state, an audit trail, long-running control, or permissions enforced outside the model, an application is a better fit. Keep project configuration out of the skill We don’t want to hardcode every project’s names, database, or conventions into the skills. In the Data Forge support-desk example, a manifest describes the project, metric store, and platform so the skills can use the right project details without baking them into their instructions: project: name: "support-desk" store_name: "support_metric_store" platform: engine: "duckdb" pipeline_framework: "spark_python" duckdb_dir: "warehouse" With the discovered details in the resolved manifest, the other skills don’t have to make their own assumptions about the project. Keep discovered project details separate from team standards. The forge-init initialization skill can inspect existing schemas and code patterns; the forge-lint skill supplies the rules to follow before code is generated. A pattern found in a repository isn’t automatically a rule to preserve, so make discovered details reviewable and let people confirm or change them where business judgment is needed. To check portability, ask: could another team use these skills with its own manifest without rewriting them? Share execution paths between skills The forge-dbx skill gives the other Data Forge skills one way to access the data platform. It reads the manifest and selects a Databricks or DuckDB adapter, so each skill doesn’t need its own connection and query logic. The manifest can choose DuckDB for the local support-desk demo, but it can’t install the DuckDB CLI or grant database access. Those remain setup responsibilities for the environment and its user. The manifest picks the engine; the host provides the access. Put checks and approval points in the workflow The Data Forge support-desk workflow has seven phases, with a human checkpoint at each one. The workflow overview shows how the skills fit together. Before a phase proceeds, the workflow checks that the previous phase is complete; before schema changes run, it asks for approval. The Proof Agent example applies the same principle to code review. A GitHub Actions workflow gives the verifier the original request and code changes, but not the coding agent’s own assessment. The verifier returns PASS , FAIL , or PARTIAL and must cite evidence in the changed files. The GitHub Action does a static review of the diff; it doesn’t execute code or run tests. In the demo workflow, we set block-on-fail: false so findings were advisory. By default, a FAIL fails the check, which blocks the merge if the check is required. The aim is to keep test results and merge requirements in your repository’s CI checks and rules. Package for each agent client, then verify its setup Supporting multiple clients can mean keeping several copies of the same instructions in sync.

articles.title: Build once, run on any agent: A practical guide to agent skills
articles.headline: GitHub introduces agent skills for reusable AI workflows
articles.summary: GitHub Blog announces agent skills, versioned directories centered on SKILL.md files that capture repeatable instructions for AI agents. The feature allows teams to define tasks with clear inputs and outputs, coordinate multiple skills in workflows like Data Forge, and share execution paths via a manifest. Skills can describe tasks such as database queries or code verification, though the environment must still provide necessary tools and permissions. The approach aims to reduce context loss and institutional knowledge silos by enabling reusable, portable workflows across different agents and projects.

articles.content: Spend controls have been at the top of the list of most requested features from developers building on our developer platform for quite some time now. With more than 10 million developers now building on Cloudflare, this matters more than ever. Although we’ve had usage notifications and budget alerts available to paid plans for a while, this doesn’t solve the problem completely; informing is not the same as controlling. You can now set spending thresholds and choose to have Cloudflare pause activity when those limits are reached, thus avoiding unexpected bills from unplanned usage. Today, we're introducing Spend Management in Beta, for any pay-as-you-go (PayGo) customer, starting with Workers and Durable Objects. Use Spend Management alongside AI Gateway spend limits to manage compute and AI inference costs across your application. AI Gateway already supports per-user and per-model budgets for Workers AI and other AI providers, applied to requests routed through your gateway. How it works You can start using Spend Management using the dashboard, cf CLI , or REST API . In the dashboard , head over to Manage Account > Billing > Spend limits and enable the products for which you want to control spending. When you enable controls on a product, you can define a spending limit, specify a recipient email for notifications, and set one or more alert thresholds. If you configure a recipient email, Cloudflare will send notifications when the evaluated spend reaches one of the thresholds or your spending limit. When the limit is reached, a blocking policy is enforced and your product is paused automatically. If you go to the dashboard , you can see the current billing cycle costs for each supported product in near real time (under 10 minutes), and manage your settings and thresholds from there. The overview panel tells you which products have thresholds and limits configured. In this example, you can see that Workers triggered two alerts before hitting the hard limit. Note that the billing cycle starts when the paid subscription begins, not when you deploy a Worker or create a spending cap; a subscription starting October 10 generally has a cycle of October 10-November 10 — not a calendar month. The dashboard also shows an audit log, so you can see who changed a limit and when, or when a cap was reached. As with most Cloudflare services, Spend Management is also an API that you can use programmatically; the documentation can be found in our Developer Documentation . Here’s an example, but using the API: curl --fail-with-body --request POST \ "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/${CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID}/billing/spend-policies" \ --header "Authorization: Bearer ${CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN}" \ --header "Content-Type: application/json" \ --data '{ "name": "Workers spending cap", "product_id": "workers", "enabled": true, "threshold_cents": 10000, "action": "usage_block", "notification_email": "me@example.com" }' And, of course, you can use cf, the CLI for the entire Cloudflare API : cf billing spend-policies list cf billing spend-policies create cf billing spend-policies get cf billing spend-policies update cf billing spend-policies delete cf billing spend-policies audit list cf billing spend-policies activity list cf billing spend-policies create --body '{ "name": "Workers spending cap", "product_id": "workers", "enabled": true, "threshold_cents": 10000, "action": "usage_block", "notification_email": "me@example.com" }' Once a cap is enforced, new invocations of that product are rejected. Note that we only pause customer-code invocations that incur costs — in Workers, for example, Cron Triggers and Queue consumer invocations are paused, but static assets continue to be served. To resume service, you can: Raise the limit above the current cycle’s accumulated spend. Disable or delete the blocking policy. Wait until the next billing cycle, when the existing block expires. That’s it. You can start using Spend Management for Workers and Durable Objects today, and other products will follow soon. Read on to learn how we built the system, and what’s going to happen next. How we built Spend Management As easy and straightforward as it seems on the surface, building a system like this at Cloudflare scale was no small feat. From an invocation anywhere on our distributed network to a blocking decision that we need to apply globally, building Spend Management required working with multiple teams, changing code in existing systems, and creating new systems from scratch. Let’s start by looking at the bird's-eye view of a capped billable event: Now let's dig deeper. Collecting and aggregating close to the source Each invocation produces usage measurements: requests, CPU time, execution duration, or storage operations, depending on the product. But transporting and processing this volume of raw data all the way from the sources down to the rating engine would not scale or be efficient. So what we do is we collect and aggregate the measurements as close to the source as possible using a two-stage metering pipeline that combines events into usage aggregates, so the engine sees accumulated usage rather than having to process all the events one by one. Let's look at a diagram. The first stage reduces raw-event volume close to parsing down to one-minute windows. Each metering parser converts raw events into usage measurements, then combines matching measurements into typically one-minute buckets. Still, several records can describe the same account and time window. In the second stage, a separate service merges those first-stage partial aggregates using the same grouping rules, but over typically five-minute windows, and further reduces the volume before downstream processing by the Usage Engine. Here we also archive the consolidated aggregates; this gives us a durable dataset for later analytics and reconciliation. The nice thing about this two-stage pipeline is that it reduces the raw event volume early, so the downstream engines process only the aggregated usage they need to calculate spend and act on it. That’s what makes this practical at Cloudflare’s scale. Usage Engine: account-partitioned processing The Usage Engine translates aggregated measurements into usage records, which are standardized records containing the account, usage window, metric, quantity, and relevant dimensions. In other words, it maps product-specific meters into supported usage metrics. We partition processing by account, so an account’s usage and subscription information meet in the same place.
articles.excerpt: Spend controls have been at the top of the list of most requested features from developers building on our developer platform for quite some time now. With more than 10 million developers now building on Cloudflare, this matters more than ever.
articles.title: Introducing Spend Management: Spending limits and alerts for Cloudflare
articles.headline: Cloudflare launches Spend Management beta for pay-as-you-go customers
articles.summary: Cloudflare introduces Spend Management in beta for pay-as-you-go customers, allowing them to set spending limits and alerts to avoid unexpected bills. The feature starts with Workers and Durable Objects, enabling users to define thresholds that pause product activity when reached. The system uses a two-stage metering pipeline to aggregate usage data efficiently at scale. Users can configure limits and notifications via dashboard, CLI, or API, with the Rating Engine calculating spend based on usage metrics and subscription allowances. The feature aims to give developers control over compute and AI inference costs across their applications.

articles.content: Dados de 2026 revelam uma desaceleração nas oportunidades para engenheiros de software e um crescimento expressivo nas vagas de gerenciamento de produtos. O que está acontecendo com o mercado de trabalho em tecnologia? Durante anos, a engenharia de software foi uma das áreas mais promissoras do mercado profissional. A transformação digital, a expansão das startups, a computação em nuvem e a popularização dos aplicativos criaram uma demanda crescente por desenvolvedores. Entretanto, os indicadores mais recentes do mercado global de tecnologia apontam para uma mudança significativa nesse cenário. Segundo levantamento apresentado por Lenny Rachitsky em novembro de 2026, com dados da TrueUp e da Live Data Technologies, o crescimento das vagas abertas para profissionais de engenharia de software em empresas de tecnologia caiu drasticamente. Depois de crescer 29% em 2024 e 15% em 2025, o número de oportunidades avançou apenas 2,5% em 2026. Enquanto isso, as vagas para gerentes de produto ( Product Managers ) atingiram o maior patamar em quase quatro anos. Essa diferença merece atenção. Não estamos necessariamente diante do desaparecimento da engenharia de software, mas de uma possível transformação na maneira como as empresas organizam suas equipes, desenvolvem produtos e distribuem responsabilidades. 1. A desaceleração da engenharia de software Os números apresentados por Rachitsky mostram uma redução progressiva no ritmo de expansão das oportunidades profissionais. Ano Crescimento das vagas de engenharia 2024 +29% 2025 +15% 2026 +2,5% A desaceleração é expressiva. Em dois anos, o crescimento anual das vagas perdeu grande parte de sua força. O cenário fica ainda mais interessante quando observamos as contratações efetivamente realizadas nos Estados Unidos. Entre maio de 2025 e abril de 2026, aproximadamente 113 mil engenheiros de software foram contratados. Em 2022, durante o período de maior expansão do setor, esse número chegou a 239 mil. Isso significa que o volume recente representa menos da metade do pico registrado quatro anos antes. Outro indicador reforça a tendência: embora as oportunidades anunciadas para engenharia tenham crescido 44% desde janeiro de 2024, as contratações efetivas recuaram 17% no mesmo período. Essa diferença revela um problema importante para quem procura emprego: a existência de uma vaga não significa necessariamente que a empresa esteja conseguindo ou efetivamente realizando a contratação. Também pode indicar processos seletivos mais exigentes, mudanças nas prioridades corporativas ou maior cautela na expansão das equipes. 2. Product Managers: a outra face do mercado Enquanto a engenharia apresenta sinais de estabilização, o gerenciamento de produtos segue uma trajetória diferente. De acordo com o levantamento, as vagas abertas para Product Managers atingiram o maior nível em quase quatro anos, ficando 75% acima da mínima registrada em março de 2023. Desde o início de 2023, o crescimento acumulado das oportunidades foi: Product Management: +56%. Engenharia de software: +43%. A diferença pode parecer pequena à primeira vista, mas representa uma mudança relevante na distribuição das oportunidades dentro das empresas de tecnologia. Existe também outro dado interessante: entre as cinco categorias profissionais analisadas, Product Management foi a única cuja participação nas contratações aumentou, passando de 16% em 2021 para 21% em 2026. Entretanto, é necessário fazer uma distinção: o aumento das vagas anunciadas não significa que as contratações de Product Managers tenham crescido na mesma proporção. O próprio levantamento aponta estabilidade ou retração nas contratações de diversas funções de produto. A interpretação de Rachitsky é que encontrar profissionais de produto qualificados pode estar se tornando mais difícil. Isso levanta uma questão: por que empresas que estão desacelerando a contratação de engenheiros continuam demonstrando interesse em profissionais responsáveis pela estratégia e pela gestão de produtos? 3. A inteligência artificial está mudando a divisão do trabalho? Uma das explicações possíveis está na popularização das ferramentas de inteligência artificial. Ferramentas de programação assistida, modelos de linguagem e agentes capazes de executar tarefas técnicas estão modificando a produtividade das equipes de desenvolvimento. Atividades que anteriormente exigiam horas de implementação podem ser realizadas em menos tempo, especialmente quando envolvem código repetitivo, testes, documentação e prototipação. Isso não significa que a inteligência artificial substituiu a engenharia de software. Significa que o custo e o tempo necessários para determinadas atividades estão mudando. Uma equipe menor pode conseguir entregar funcionalidades que anteriormente exigiriam mais profissionais, desde que tenha processos adequados, conhecimento técnico e capacidade de revisão. Nesse contexto, a empresa pode passar a valorizar ainda mais profissionais capazes de identificar problemas, definir prioridades, compreender usuários e transformar necessidades de negócio em soluções viáveis. É justamente nesse espaço que o Product Manager ganha relevância. O profissional não é responsável apenas por organizar tarefas ou manter um backlog atualizado. Seu trabalho envolve decisões sobre o que desenvolver, por que desenvolver, para quem desenvolver e como avaliar os resultados. Com a implementação de ferramentas de IA, a execução técnica pode ficar mais rápida, mas decidir corretamente o que deve ser construído continua sendo um problema complexo. Existe, porém, uma ressalva: os dados apresentados não demonstram que a inteligência artificial seja a causa direta da desaceleração das contratações de engenheiros. Ela é uma hipótese relevante para interpretar o movimento, mas fatores econômicos, reorganizações corporativas e mudanças no investimento em tecnologia também podem influenciar os resultados. 4. O engenheiro de software do futuro precisará ir além do código? Uma consequência possível dessa transformação é a mudança no perfil profissional procurado pelas empresas. Durante muito tempo, dominar linguagens de programação, frameworks, bancos de dados e arquitetura de software foi suficiente para construir uma carreira competitiva. Essas competências continuam fundamentais. Entretanto, o mercado parece caminhar para uma valorização maior da capacidade de resolver problemas completos. Um desenvolvedor que compreende o funcionamento do negócio, participa de decisões arquiteturais, conhece as necessidades dos usuários e consegue avaliar o impacto de uma funcionalidade possui uma visão mais abrangente do produto. Isso não significa que todos os engenheiros devam migrar para Product Management. Na realidade, a especialização técnica continua sendo necessária. Sistemas distribuídos, segurança, infraestrutura, confiabilidade, desempenho e arquitetura de software envolvem problemas que não desaparecem com a popularização da IA.

O que está acontecendo com o mercado de trabalho em tecnologia? Durante anos, a engenharia de software foi uma das áreas mais promissoras do mercado profissional.

articles.content: Olá, pessoal! Gostaria de apresentar um projeto que comecei recentemente: o Tech Briefing , um boletim independente de divulgação de oportunidades de trabalho, inicialmente com foco no mercado de tecnologia. A ideia surgiu de uma situação bastante comum: encontrar uma vaga interessante nem sempre é tão simples quanto parece. Existem diversas plataformas, comunidades e canais de divulgação, mas as oportunidades acabam ficando espalhadas por diferentes lugares. Às vezes, uma boa vaga passa despercebida simplesmente porque não chegamos até ela. Foi pensando nisso que resolvi criar uma alternativa para reunir e compartilhar essas oportunidades. O que é o Tech Briefing? Imagine aqueles antigos classificados de jornal, nos quais as pessoas procuravam oportunidades de emprego. A proposta é trazer um pouco dessa ideia para o ambiente digital. O Tech Briefing funciona como um boletim de vagas, reunindo oportunidades encontradas em diferentes fontes e organizando suas principais informações para facilitar a consulta. Não somos responsáveis pelos processos seletivos e muito menos pelas contratações. Nosso papel é encontrar, organizar e divulgar oportunidades que já existem. Também temos uma preocupação importante com a qualidade das informações: não inventamos requisitos, salários, benefícios ou descrições. Procuramos preservar o máximo possível das informações disponibilizadas pela própria empresa ou pelo responsável pela divulgação da vaga. Onde você pode acompanhar? Atualmente, estamos trabalhando com três plataformas de divulgação e também compartilhando oportunidades em outras redes sociais. A ideia é justamente não limitar o projeto a um único canal. Se você prefere acompanhar as oportunidades pelo Telegram, Discord ou receber atualizações por e-mail, queremos explorar essas possibilidades. Não queremos que as pessoas precisem se adaptar ao projeto. Queremos que o projeto consiga alcançar as pessoas onde elas já estão. Inclusive, sugestões de novas plataformas, ferramentas e formas de distribuição são muito bem-vindas nos comentários. Empresas, projetos e comunidades também podem participar Outro ponto importante: o Tech Briefing não é exclusivo para grandes empresas. Se você é uma empresa, uma startup, um MEI, participa de um projeto independente ou conhece alguém que esteja procurando pessoas para trabalhar, pode entrar em contato para divulgar uma oportunidade. Aceitamos sugestões de vagas em diferentes modalidades, incluindo: Oportunidades CLT e PJ; Estágios e programas de trainee; Trabalhos freelancers; Projetos independentes; Oportunidades voluntárias; Outras modalidades de colaboração. Queremos facilitar a circulação dessas oportunidades, inclusive daquelas que normalmente não recebem tanta visibilidade. Se você encontrou uma vaga interessante e não sabe onde divulgá-la, pode entrar em contato comigo pelo LinkedIn ou por alguma das minhas redes sociais. Um projeto independente, em construção É importante deixar claro que o Tech Briefing é um projeto independente. Não recebemos financiamento de empresas, não cobramos para divulgar oportunidades e não temos vínculo comercial com as organizações responsáveis pelas vagas. Isso também significa que não garantimos a legitimidade de todos os processos seletivos. Procuramos verificar as informações disponíveis e evitar oportunidades suspeitas ou problemáticas, mas recomendamos que os candidatos sempre confiram os detalhes diretamente nos canais oficiais das empresas. Nosso objetivo inicial é publicar aproximadamente cinco oportunidades por dia. Ainda estamos longe dessa meta: atualmente, temos um volume bastante pequeno de divulgações. Mas todo projeto começa de algum lugar, e acredito que começar com uma oportunidade já é melhor do que não compartilhar nenhuma. O que vem pela frente? Apesar de o projeto ter começado com foco em tecnologia, não quero necessariamente limitar o Tech Briefing a esse mercado. Existem oportunidades interessantes em diversas áreas, e seria muito legal conseguir ampliar esse alcance futuramente. Também queremos melhorar a organização das vagas, explorar novas plataformas de distribuição e encontrar maneiras de tornar a experiência de acompanhamento mais simples. E, principalmente, queremos ouvir quem está do outro lado. Se você acompanha o projeto, tem alguma sugestão, encontrou um problema ou acredita que poderíamos fazer algo diferente, fique à vontade para comentar. Não temos a pretensão de reinventar a divulgação de vagas. A proposta é contribuir de uma maneira simples com comunidades das quais já participo ou das quais pretendo participar. Acredito que iniciativas assim também são uma boa maneira de aproximar pessoas, compartilhar conhecimento e construir conexões. O Tech Briefing está apenas começando. Obrigado por ter lido até aqui e, se conhecer alguém procurando uma oportunidade, compartilhe o projeto! Até a próxima!

articles.content: Short answer: make the retrieval contract explicit, keep durable policy in a vector index, use live web retrieval only for freshness, and degrade to a cited cached answer when a dependency times out. That boundary is what makes failure recovery testable for a healthcare appointment assistant. Start with the answer contract An appointment assistant should not begin with a vendor choice. Begin with the answer a patient can safely act on. For every response, define which facts must be current (clinic hours, appointment slots, holiday closures), which can be durable (approved preparation instructions), and what citation or document identifier the reviewer needs to see. I write that down as a small contract: freshness , authority , latency_budget , and evidence . A request for “Can I book Tuesday at 3?” needs live availability and a source URL or record ID. “How should I prepare?” can use an indexed clinical document, provided its revision is current and the assistant returns that document ID. If the contract cannot be met, the assistant should ask a narrower question or hand off; it should not fill the gap with a confident guess. This also gives the on-call engineer a useful failure signal. A timeout is not one generic error. It says which contract field was missed and whether a fallback is safe. For teams that want one plain HTTP surface around several backend capabilities, Infrai is a practical option to evaluate at this boundary: one key and one bill cover the retrieval calls, and the same REST convention can sit beside other services without an SDK install. Its public discovery endpoint exposes request schemas and runnable examples, so an adapter can follow declared paths instead of guessed REST shapes. I've found that boundary easier to review during an incident, though it still needs the same clinical governance as any other provider. How should a healthcare appointment assistant recover retrieval failures? Treat each source as a bounded step. Set an explicit timeout, cap the number of candidates, and retry only transient failures with exponential backoff. A slow web page must not hold the patient flow open while a worker waits forever. For live pages, retain the last verified snapshot with its retrieval timestamp; for durable records, keep the previous index generation until the replacement has been checked. The recovery order I use is deliberately boring: Try the source that satisfies the contract (vector or live web). On a timeout or rate limit, retry within the request budget. If freshness is still required, return a clear “needs confirmation” handoff rather than stale availability. If the contract permits a snapshot, answer from it and expose its URL or document ID. That distinction matters. A cached clinic policy is a reasonable fallback; a cached appointment slot is not. Your mileage may vary with the booking system's own consistency guarantees, so record that assumption in the runbook. The application should own the contract and policy. The retrieval provider should return passages plus provenance. This makes a provider swap a boundary change instead of a rewrite of booking logic. Here is a minimal Go adapter. It keeps the two paths separate so the caller can enforce the freshness contract and inspect source metadata. The payload fields shown are intentionally small; validate them against the live schema before production rollout. package main import ( "bytes" "context" "encoding/json" "fmt" "io" "net/http" "os" "time" ) func call ( ctx context . Context , path string , payload map [ string ] any ) ( [ ] byte , error ) { body , err := json . Marshal ( payload ) if err != nil { return nil , err } client := & http . Client { Timeout : 3 * time . Second } for attempt := 0 ; attempt < 3 ; attempt ++ { req , err := http . NewRequestWithContext ( ctx , "POST" , "https://api.infrai.cc" + path , bytes . NewReader ( body ) ) if err != nil { return nil , err } req . Header . Set ( "Authorization" , "Bearer " + os . Getenv ( "INFRAI_API_KEY" ) ) req . Header . Set ( "Content-Type" , "application/json" ) resp , err := client . Do ( req ) if err != nil { return nil , err } data , readErr := io . ReadAll ( resp . Body ) resp . Body . Close ( ) if readErr != nil { return nil , readErr } if resp . StatusCode == http . StatusTooManyRequests { time . Sleep ( time . Duration ( 1 << attempt ) * 200 * time . Millisecond ) continue } if resp . StatusCode < 200 || resp . StatusCode >= 300 { return nil , fmt . Errorf ( "retrieval status %d: %s" , resp . StatusCode , data ) } return data , nil } return nil , fmt . Errorf ( "rate limit persisted" ) } func main ( ) { ctx , cancel := context . WithTimeout ( context . Background ( ) , 2500 * time . Millisecond ) defer cancel ( ) vector , err := call ( ctx , "/v1/vector/query" , map [ string ] any { "query" : "clinic preparation instructions" , "limit" : 5 } ) if err != nil { fmt . Println ( "vector fallback required:" , err ) } else { fmt . Println ( string ( vector ) ) } web , err := call ( ctx , "/v1/web/search" , map [ string ] any { "query" : "clinic holiday hours" , "limit" : 5 } ) if err != nil { fmt . Println ( "live source unavailable; require confirmation:" , err ) } else { fmt . Println ( string ( web ) ) } } The important behavior is outside the HTTP call: preserve the source URL or identifier from each result, attach it to the generated answer, and make the caller decide whether stale data is acceptable.
