articles.content: Today, the Git project is releasing new versions to address six security vulnerabilities. These include arbitrary code execution when recursively cloning a malicious repository, writes to unintended files, and memory corruption when processing merges or binary patches. The fixes are included in Git 2.56.1 , with backports to Git 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. We recommend updating to Git 2.56.1 or the patched release for your maintenance series, and updating any applications that bundle Git. Vulnerabilities in Git CVE-2026-111760: Code execution during recursive clones Git checks paths before writing files into a working tree, including rejecting paths that would overwrite its own repository metadata. However, an integer truncation in Git’s index handling can cause an extremely long path to pass validation under one name and then be written using a shorter name. An attacker can use this discrepancy to replace a submodule’s .git file with a symbolic link pointing to a directory containing malicious configuration or hooks . When Git subsequently uses that directory, it can execute attacker-controlled code during a recursive clone. The fix rejects extremely long index entry paths before their lengths can be truncated. [ Advisory ] CVE-2026-113408: Path traversal through a server’s advertised HEAD When cloning an empty repository using Git protocol v2, the server can advertise a HEAD symref pointing to an unborn branch (one that has no commits yet). Git did not validate the symref’s target before storing it locally. A malicious server can supply a name containing path-traversal components. With the files reference backend, a later operation that updates the branch can write outside the intended reference directory. Git now validates the advertised target before accepting it. The release also validates other reference names and symbolic-reference targets received through protocol v2. [ Advisory ] CVE-2026-114467: Stack corruption when removing signatures When stripping GPG signatures from a message, Git assumed there would be at most two signatures. A specially crafted message containing more than two signatures can cause Git to write past the end of a fixed-size stack array. This can be triggered by merging a tag containing more than two signatures, causing memory corruption and a potential denial of service. Hosting services that perform these merges on behalf of users can also be affected. The fix removes the fixed-size array and handles messages with any number of signatures. [ Advisory ] CVE-2026-114469: Out-of-bounds reads when applying binary patches Git rejects patches larger than approximately 1 GiB because its patch application code cannot safely handle larger inputs. However, this check only considered the size of the patch as supplied. Binary patches are compressed and encoded, so a relatively small patch can expand beyond that limit. A crafted patch can bypass the input-size check and cause an out-of-bounds read, crashing Git. Git now also checks the declared uncompressed size before processing a binary patch. [ Advisory ] CVE-2026-105437: Heap corruption during large merges Git’s merge machinery calculates how much memory it needs for a merge result before writing the output. That calculation can overflow when the result is very large, including when many conflicts are combined with a large conflict-marker-size attribute. The overflow can cause Git to allocate a buffer that is too small, then write outside it, corrupting heap memory. This affects applications and hosting services that use Git to merge untrusted content, as well as local merges. The fix uses size-appropriate types and checked arithmetic, rejecting merges whose output size cannot be represented safely. [ Advisory ] CVE-2026-114466: Filesystem access through fast-import streams git fast-import reads a stream of commands to build a repository. Some commands can access files outside the repository, so Git already restricts them when they appear in an untrusted input stream. Three additional features lacked that protection. The rewrite-submodules-from and rewrite-submodules-to features can read arbitrary files, potentially exposing their contents through error messages. The export-pack-edges option can create files or append data to existing files. These features are now rejected when supplied through the input stream unless the caller explicitly enables --allow-unsafe-features . Only enable that option when you trust the program generating the stream. [ Advisory ] Additional hardening Alongside these fixes, the release adds overflow checks to related index entry allocations during checkout and tree processing. These checks complement the path-length limits above, preventing allocation sizes from being truncated or overflowing before Git copies a path into memory. Protecting GitHub users We have deployed fixes for these vulnerabilities across github.com, GitHub Enterprise Cloud, and GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency. Updates for GitHub Enterprise Server are available in versions 3.19.15, 3.20.11, 3.21.9, and 3.22.4. We recommend that administrators upgrade as soon as possible. We are coordinating releases of GitHub Desktop and the GitHub Copilot app that include patched versions of Git. GitHub Codespaces and GitHub Actions will also receive patched versions of Git. Update Git Updating is the most effective way to protect against these vulnerabilities. Install a patched version from your operating system or Git distributor, and update applications that include their own copy of Git. Administrators should also update Git installations used by automation and services that process repositories on behalf of users. If you cannot update immediately, clone only from trusted servers and avoid recursive clones of untrusted repositories. Avoid merging untrusted content or tags, or processing binary patches or fast-import streams from untrusted sources. These precautions do not replace installing the fixes. Get an updated version of Git >

articles.content: Cloudflare recently announced Meerkat , an experimental distributed consensus service designed to manage our internal global control plane. It is powered by a new consensus algorithm published by researchers Tennage & Băsescu et al. called QuePaxa (2023). QuePaxa is an unusual choice; most consensus systems use well-established consensus algorithms like Raft, (Multi-)Paxos or Viewstamped Replication. These algorithms are well understood, have mature implementations, and usually work well. Unfortunately, common consensus algorithms often suffer in wide-area networks with volatile network connectivity and latency, i.e., networks like the Internet, which is where Meerkat runs. These algorithms rely on a single leader process being available and having predictable latency. If the leader goes down, experiences higher latency than usual, or is disconnected, the entire consensus system slows down or becomes unavailable until the leader is replaced. This is unacceptable for Meerkat. Meerkat’s global deployment environment led us to a newer consensus algorithm, QuePaxa, which promises better stability despite volatility, in large part by not relying on a leader to make progress. In this post we’ll explain why we chose QuePaxa and how the QuePaxa algorithm works. What we’re building and why it’s unique Meerkat is a distributed system in which replicas agree upon an ordered log of events, where each event is decided by a consensus algorithm. Consensus algorithms allow a group of machines to agree on a single shared truth, even if some of those machines crash or disconnect. Consensus algorithms provide an important guarantee: machines never decide conflicting values. This ensures Meerkat replicas’ logs never diverge. Meerkat uses its consensus-powered log to expose applications like a key-value store, where each entry in the log is a get or a put . Because the consensus algorithm guarantees replicas’ logs never diverge, they all construct the same key-value (KV) state. Comparable consensus-powered systems include Consul, etcd, and Apache ZooKeeper. Unlike similar systems, however, Meerkat was designed for global scale . A Meerkat cluster may be distributed across continents and connected by links that often exhibit high and variable latency. This is an unusual setup for consensus systems, which are usually deployed in smaller, more local networks, and have strict latency requirements . The challenges of consensus at a global scale While all consensus algorithms ensure that replicas agree on the same value, many of them become disproportionately unavailable or slow when network conditions degrade (but machines do not crash). We have seen this happen firsthand: in 2020, the partial failure of a core Cloudflare network switch caused a consensus-powered system to degrade and the dashboard to operate 80x slower than usual, for six hours. Critically, the system lost no data. But it became unavailable for writes until the issue was resolved, which is unacceptable. Ideally, a consensus algorithm should be able to make progress despite latency spikes and broken connections, not just replica failures. This is particularly a problem at global scale, where faults are more likely to originate in the network, and not our own servers. Let’s examine two common traits of consensus algorithms that can lead to degradation under hostile network conditions: destructive interference and fault detection. Later, we’ll see how QuePaxa sidesteps both of these issues. Destructive interference and leaders Consider Paxos, the veritable grandfather of most consensus algorithms. A lot of consensus algorithms inherit the structure of Paxos – both the good and the not-so-good bits. Leaving an egregious amount of detail out, here’s how Paxos works. There are two kinds of processes: proposers and acceptors. Abstractly, the goal of the system is for a majority of acceptors to agree on a value proposed by some proposer. There are two phases: the Prepare phase, and the Accept phase. In the Prepare phase, any proposer can send a ballot number out to a majority of acceptors. This ballot number serves as a promise – acceptors will only accept proposals with that ballot number or higher. Then, in the Accept phase, the proposer sends its proposal along with the ballot number to a majority of acceptors again. If a majority of acceptors still hold the ballot number of the proposal, the majority accepts it, and the proposer can safely decide the proposal. Challenges arise when two or more proposers submit proposals at the same time. Specifically, another proposer can interleave its own higher ballot number in between the two phases, blocking any lower ballots. Two proposers can repeatedly block each other from progressing – effectively competing for acceptance. When proposers compete and block each other in this way, we say that they destructively interfere. Destructive interference gets worse as more proposers propose their own ballots. The more concurrent proposers there are, the more likely it is that the system gets stuck repeatedly proposing. Even if none of the replicas have crashed or are unavailable, multiple proposers and misbehaving networks can block Paxos. Formally, we say that Paxos does not guarantee liveness (i.e., that proposals are eventually decided) without assuming that, at some point, all messages arrive within a bounded amount of time — an assumption known as partial synchrony. To avoid multiple proposers constantly competing, most deployed consensus algorithms, like Raft, Multi-Paxos, and Viewstamped Replication, add a special leader proposer. The leader is the only replica that can make proposals. Centralizing the proposing power in one replica forces an order on concurrent requests, avoids competing proposals, and has the added benefit of getting decisions done in an optimal single network round-trip, instead of two. While the leader is healthy and the network is well-behaved, leader-based protocols are fast. The trade-off is that the leader must remain operational and reachable. When it fails, becomes too slow, or is disconnected from the cluster, the system stalls. The only solution is for the remaining replicas to detect that the leader has failed, and elect a new one in its place. When leader recovery is unstable When a leader fails, the system must recover by electing a new one. Interestingly, leader recovery is often how destructive interference sneaks right back into a leader-based system.

articles.title: Choosing QuePaxa, an unusual consensus algorithm
articles.headline: Cloudflare announces Meerkat, experimental distributed consensus service powered by QuePaxa algorithm
articles.summary: Cloudflare announced Meerkat, an experimental distributed consensus service designed to manage its internal global control plane. Powered by the new QuePaxa consensus algorithm, Meerkat addresses limitations of traditional leader-based systems like Raft and Paxos, which degrade under wide-area network volatility. Unlike established algorithms relying on a single leader, QuePaxa promises better stability by avoiding destructive interference and inaccurate fault detection. The system ensures replicas maintain consistent logs despite high latency and broken connections, preventing the unavailability and performance degradation seen in previous Cloudflare incidents.

articles.content: Latchkey vs BuildJet is no longer a comparison you can act on: BuildJet announced the shutdown of BuildJet for GitHub Actions on 6 February 2026 and stopped running jobs on 31 March 2026. What is left is a migration, so this page is about the buildjet-* labels still sitting in workflow files and what the surviving options cost against the rate you used to pay. The same month at each rate: 10,000 Linux minutes at 2 vCPU plus 2,000 macOS minutes, which BuildJet never sold either. Rates read 20 September 2026; the BuildJet bar is the rate its frozen page still shows. BuildJet sold managed runners on its own bare metal, adopted with a one-line runs-on change, at $0.004 a minute for 2 vCPU and 8 GB rising to $0.048 for 32 vCPU. It published arm64 variants of every size and a drop-in cache action with 20 GB per repository per week, which was double the GitHub-hosted allowance. Its site is still up and still shows that rate card, under a banner reading "BuildJet for GitHub Actions has been shut down", so do not price your migration from it. Latchkey sells managed runners the same way, at $0.0025 a minute for 2 vCPU and 8 GB, with a dependency cache that replaces buildjet/cache with a restore step and a save step, and transient failures repaired on the runner. It is the closest thing on price to what BuildJet was, and it is missing the thing a good share of BuildJet users were there for: there is no arm64, Windows or macOS runner, so an arm64 job has to land somewhere else. Every cell below was read from the vendor's own public pricing or documentation page on 20 September 2026. Where a vendor does not publish a number, the cell says "not published" instead of carrying a guess. Comparison BuildJet (ended 31 March 2026) GitHub-hosted Latchkey Price per minute, 2 vCPU Linux x64 $0.004 (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM), on a frozen page $0.006 (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 14 GB SSD on a private repo; free on public repos) $0.0025 (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 100 GB disk) Price per minute, 4 vCPU Linux x64 $0.008 (4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM) $0.012 as a larger runner $0.005 (4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 100 GB disk) Free tier None published; concurrency subscriptions were made free on 6 February 2026 as the service wound down $12 of compute a month on Free, $18 on Pro and Team, $300 on Enterprise Cloud (2,000, 3,000 and 50,000 standard Linux minutes), private repos only 30-day trial, then 2,000 included minutes a month on Developer, 4,000 on Launch, 6,000 on Scale Billing granularity Per minute Every job is rounded up to the nearest whole minute Per minute Runner sizes and OS 2 to 32 vCPU on Ubuntu 22.04, x64 and arm64 Linux x64 and arm64, Windows x64 and arm64, macOS; larger runners to 96 vCPU 2, 4, 8 and 16 vCPU, Ubuntu 24.04 on x86_64 only. arm64, Windows and macOS are not offered Cache: type, limit, persistence BuildJet Cache, 20 GB per repo per week free, interoperable with actions/cache actions/cache , 10 GB per repository, entries removed after 7 days without access Size not published. latchkey-dev/cache-action@v1 replaces actions/cache with a restore step and a save step, keeping path and key (no restore-keys ); entries are isolated per organization, versioned by OS, kept 14 days; a failed restore warns rather than failing the job Docker build acceleration BuildJet Cache in front of buildx; no managed layer-cache service after shutdown None built in. cache-to: type=gha writes into the same 10 GB store latchkey-dev/docker-cache-action@v1 , layers held in a Latchkey-managed private registry per organization Concurrency limits Sold as a concurrency subscription, then made free during the wind-down 20 concurrent jobs on Free, 40 on Pro, 60 on Team, 500 on Enterprise Cloud. macOS is capped separately at 5, or 50 on Enterprise Developer 20, Launch 40, Scale 80 busy runners per workspace; idle warm runners do not count Where jobs run BuildJet's own bare metal, until 31 March 2026 GitHub's own hosted fleet Latchkey's own AWS estate on m6a-class hosts, one job per runner, no inbound access, destroyed after the job Self-healing or retries Not offered None. A failed job waits for a person, or for retry logic you wrote yourself Built in: transient failures are diagnosed and retried inside the run Setup change required A runs-on label change, now a label that resolves to nothing None; this is the default A runs-on label change. GitHub organization accounts only What happened, and what it means for your workflow files BuildJet posted the notice on 6 February 2026: new signups closed that day, all concurrency subscriptions became free, pay-as-you-go billing continued as normal, and on 31 March 2026 the runners stopped taking jobs. The company's own migration advice was to move to GitHub-hosted runners, use GitHub's native arm64 runners for arm workflows, and swap the BuildJet cache action back to actions/cache , which it describes as interoperable. If a buildjet-* label is still in a workflow file today, the job does not fail loudly with a helpful message. It queues, waiting for a runner with that label to appear, until it hits the job timeout or somebody cancels it. That is worth grepping for across every repository and every branch that still builds, including the ones nobody has touched since March. The label map Every BuildJet size maps to something, but not to one thing: GitHub sells its 4 vCPU and larger sizes as larger runners with labels you define yourself in organization settings, so there is no drop-in string to paste. Prices are per minute, read 20 September 2026.

articles.content: Background: Why We Needed a Simulator Initially, we started writing code with a casual mindset: "We can just add a random number within ±20% of the base TTL." However, during stress testing in our QA environment, two critical issues surfaced: Runaway Negative and Zero TTLs : When the random jitter width ( jitter_range ) exceeded the base TTL ( base_ttl ), the calculated TTL became 0 or negative, causing immediate key eviction or errors on the Redis side. Fragile JSON Parsing and Exception Handling : When invalid types or malformed payloads were fed into the system, Python's standard json module made it difficult to return structured, detailed validation errors, undermining its reliability as a CLI tool. We needed to stop implementing jitter based on "gut feeling" and establish a CLI tool in code that enforces strict input validation, guarantees safety in edge cases, and quantitatively verifies the distribution of generated TTLs. Architecture and Verification Flow This tool accepts JSON-formatted configuration values as input, passes them through strict type-safe validation via Pydantic, and calculates and aggregates jittered TTLs for the specified number of requests. sequenceDiagram participant CLI as "External Process / CLI" participant Core as "run_simulation()" participant Validator as "Pydantic (SimulationConfig)" participant Calc as "calculate_jittered_ttl()" CLI->>Core: "JSON bytes (config_json)" Core->>Validator: "orjson.loads() & Model Instantiation" alt "Validation Error / Malformed JSON" Validator-->>Core: "ValidationError / JSONDecodeError" Core-->>CLI: "Error JSON (status: ERROR)" else "Success Path" Validator-->>Core: "SimulationConfig Instance" loop "For each request (request_count)" Core->>Calc: "base_ttl, jitter_range" Calc-->>Core: "Jittered TTL (min 1s guaranteed)" end Core->>Core: "Distribution aggregation & stats (min, max, avg, unique)" Core-->>CLI: "Success JSON (SimulationResult)" end Implementation The following code is a complete, standalone script that uses high-speed orjson for input serialization/deserialization and Pydantic v2 for data structure definition and validation. import random import sys from typing import List , Optional import orjson from pydantic import BaseModel , Field , field_validator , ValidationError class SimulationConfig ( BaseModel ) : base_ttl : int = Field ( . . . , gt = 0 , description = "Base expiration time in seconds" ) jitter_range : int = Field ( . . . , ge = 0 , description = "Maximum jitter range to apply in seconds" ) request_count : int = Field ( 1000 , gt = 0 , description = "Number of requests for verification" ) @field_validator ( "base_ttl" ) @classmethod def validate_base_ttl ( cls , v : int ) -> int : if v <= 0 : raise ValueError ( "base_ttl must be greater than 0" ) return v class SimulationResult ( BaseModel ) : min_ttl : int max_ttl : int average_ttl : float unique_ttl_count : int ttl_distribution : dict status : str = "SUCCESS" def calculate_jittered_ttl ( base_ttl : int , jitter_range : int ) -> int : """Applies random jitter to the base TTL.""" try : if jitter_range == 0 : return base_ttl jitter = random . randint ( - jitter_range , jitter_range ) result = base_ttl + jitter if result <= 0 : return 1 # Guarantee a minimum TTL of 1 second return result except Exception as e : raise ValueError ( f "Failed to calculate jittered TTL: {e}" ) def run_simulation ( config_json : bytes ) -> bytes : """Executes the cache stampede verification simulation and returns results via orjson.""" try : # Input validation using Pydantic config_dict = orjson . loads ( config_json ) config = SimulationConfig ( ** config_dict ) except orjson . JSONDecodeError as jde : error_res = { "status" : "ERROR" , "message" : f "Invalid JSON format: {jde}" } return orjson . dumps ( error_res ) except ValidationError as ve : error_res = { "status" : "ERROR" , "message" : f "Validation error: {ve.errors()}" } return orjson . dumps ( error_res ) except Exception as e : error_res = { "status" : "ERROR" , "message" : f "Unexpected error during parsing: {str(e)}" } return orjson . dumps ( error_res ) try : ttls : List [ int ] = [ ] for _ in range ( config . request_count ) : ttl = calculate_jittered_ttl ( config . base_ttl , config . jitter_range ) ttls . append ( ttl ) # Aggregate distribution distribution = { } for ttl in ttls : distribution [ str ( ttl ) ] = distribution . get ( str ( ttl ) , 0 ) + 1 result = SimulationResult ( min_ttl = min ( ttls ) , max_ttl = max ( ttls ) , average_ttl = sum ( ttls ) / len ( ttls ) , unique_ttl_count = len ( set ( ttls ) ) , ttl_distribution = distribution , status = "SUCCESS" ) return orjson . dumps ( result . model_dump ( ) ) except Exception as e : error_res = { "status" : "ERROR" , "message" : f "Simulation execution failed: {str(e)}" } return orjson . dumps ( error_res ) if __name__ == "__main__" : # Test payload for CLI execution sample_payload = { "base_ttl" : 300 , "jitter_range" : 60 , "request_count" : 500 } payload_bytes = orjson . dumps ( sample_payload ) output_bytes = run_simulation ( payload_bytes ) # Output results sys . stdout . buffer . write ( output_bytes ) sys . stdout . buffer . write ( b "\n" ) 💡 For immediate deployment: The complete source code suite (ZIP) for this architecture is available on Gumroad for $0+ (Pay What You Want). Key Design Points and Robustness 1. Resilience Against Edge Cases (Safeguards) In the calculate_jittered_ttl function, a fallback is implemented to forcibly return 1 second if the calculated result ever drops to 0 or below (e.g., due to misconfigured settings like base_ttl=30 and jitter_range=50 ). This prevents invalid TTLs—which could cause immediate expiration or misinterpretation as persistent keys—from ever being sent to Redis. 2. High-Speed, Strict Type Validation with Pydantic v2 and orjson Compared to the standard json module, orjson delivers superior performance.

articles.headline: New CLI tool prevents Redis cache stampede with jitter validation
articles.summary: A new Python CLI tool validates jitter parameters for Redis cache TTLs, preventing negative or zero values that cause immediate key eviction. The script uses Pydantic v2 for strict input validation and orjson for high-speed processing, guaranteeing a minimum 1-second TTL and aggregating distribution statistics across test requests to verify safety and reliability.

articles.content: Cloudflare is distributing the first $301,300 of the Vite Ecosystem Fund to 44 projects and maintainers across the Vite ecosystem. When VoidZero joined Cloudflare, we committed $1 million to strengthen the open source ecosystem around Vite. This round is just the start. Sponsoring open source has always mattered, but now AI has made funding urgent. AI is changing open source AI has made open source more valuable while triggering more maintainer burnout. Previously, contributing to a project through either an issue or pull request meant you cared about it. In return, maintainers would review and provide feedback. AI changed the social contract of open source. Anyone can now create and submit AI-authored pull requests. The most visible result is the influx of pull requests. As the number of PRs has gone up, the number of maintainers reviewing them has stayed constant. So each maintainer’s workload has grown. During reviews, maintainers often find themselves speaking with an agent and not a person like they used to. If that’s the case, then why not cut out the middleman? Maintainers now have their own agents they can prompt to produce better results since they have more knowledge of the codebase. AI has raised the pressure to produce . It’s made it easier for maintainers to ship features, performance improvements, and bug fixes that would not have been done otherwise. But it’s also made it easy for other projects to do the same. When another project adds overlapping features using AI, maintainers feel a need to keep up using AI. It can become a grinding cycle, where each project pushes the other to move faster. Along the way, some projects have grown in scope and lost sight of their original goals. Maintainer burnout and sustainability have always been a problem — and now AI has accelerated those issues. That’s why sponsoring open source projects and supporting maintainers is so important in this moment. One of the Vite Ecosystem Fund’s first recipients is e18e , a community focused on improving performance across the JavaScript ecosystem. Its lead, James Garbutt, has a long history in open source, and his work at e18e has helped make popular tools like Svelte, Storybook, and Nx faster. "Sponsorships make a huge difference and allow maintainers to dedicate more of their time to the things we all rely on," Garbutt says. Fund distribution The recipients of the Vite Ecosystem Fund were selected by a panel of core team members from Vite stack projects (Vite, Vitest, Rolldown, Oxc, Vite+), including maintainers not employed by Cloudflare. The funding is allocated through Cloudflare's Open Collective as a combination of: Contributions to ecosystem recipients Stipends to core maintainers We’re proud that Cloudflare has committed to making the open source ecosystem we rely on stronger and more sustainable. No project thrives in isolation. We'll continue to distribute and draw down the committed amount every quarter. Contributions to ecosystem recipients This first round of sponsorships prioritized dependencies, ecosystem critical plugins, significant contributors, and projects that moved the ecosystem forward. Andrew Gallant Andrey Sitnik Anthony Fu Fund Ari Perkkiö Artem Zakharchenko Babel Bart Waardenburg Benjamin E. Coe Brandon Roberts Chai David Ortner David Tolnay Denis Bardadym Devon Govett Divyansh Singh e18e ESlint Giorgio Boa Guy Bedford Jessica Sachs Jonas Kruckenberg Luigi Pinca Máximo Mussini Michael Cousins Mickael Jeanroy Misha Kaletsky Mock Service Worker Mohammad Bagher Abiyat Nicholas Rayburn Paul Miller Pig Fang pnpm Polka PostCSS Prettier Ralf Jung Rollup Sindre Sorhus Terser typescript-eslint Verite universal-deploy (Vike) Younes Jaaidi Yuki Okushi Stipends to core maintainers The core maintainers of the Vite stack are eligible for a stipend of up to $4,000 per calendar month. Each maintainer can invoice at a rate of $50 per hour contributed that month. Any time spent improving or supporting the project in some way counts towards this stipend: writing code, writing documentation, triaging issues, offering support in our Discord servers, attending meetings or meetups, contributing to our upstream dependencies, and so on. Maintainers who are already being paid for or employed for this work do not receive stipends — for example, VoidZero employees are ineligible. Cloudflare supports open source Cloudflare’s mission is to help build a better Internet. Supporting open source falls squarely within that mission. The Vite Ecosystem Fund is only part of it. Cloudflare committed an additional $1 million to sponsor open source projects in our Community Engineers Fund. We also provide Cloudflare credits to open source projects via Project Alexandria . The Vite ecosystem has come this far because of all the maintainers and contributors who came together to build a community. These sponsorships are a small thank-you for all this hard work.

articles.content: A remote flag can stop an expensive agent branch, but an incident review still needs the decision the running loop actually used. TL;DR: implement Node.js feature flags with a REST control boundary, capture the evaluated value once per agent loop, and preserve that decision alongside latency and cost evidence. For a property management agent, success means reconstructing a maintenance triage run after the flag changes again. A successful toggle proves too little. How should REST API feature flags preserve incident evidence? Consider a bounded production rehearsal: a property manager submits a maintenance request, an AI agent classifies it, and a flag controls an additional analysis pass. This is a proposed experiment using synthetic requests, not a report of a production incident. Delay one loop until after an operator changes the flag again. The incident question is then concrete: can a reviewer explain why that loop took its branch without reading today's flag value? Freeze the decision. A Node.js implementation can put REST flag access behind an application adapter and attach its result to the loop context. Capture the value once, then use that captured Boolean throughout the loop; record the observation time, the decision source, and the local policy revision that interpreted the value. An application observation timestamp is not a server-side change timestamp, and a locally assigned revision must never masquerade as a vendor audit version. Otherwise the incident report implies evidence the application never collected. For teams implementing Node.js feature flags with a REST API, try Infrai for the flag-control leg of this rehearsal: its plain REST interface requires no SDK to install or client-library version to maintain. Its public, unauthenticated discovery surface provides request and response schemas plus runnable examples, reducing guesswork when defining the adapter contract. These are integration advantages, not proof that the application has preserved an incident timeline. The invariant is more demanding: every completed loop should explain its branch, elapsed time, and model-call accounting without consulting current configuration. Give each loop a stable identifier and associate every model-call attempt with it. Preserve returned request identifiers. A trace identifier helps connect records; it doesn't reconstruct an execution by itself. Evidence comes first. Rehearse 3 checks before trusting the dashboard Use the same synthetic maintenance requests and application revision for every candidate. Assign a fresh run identifier per execution, and keep intended control changes in a separate operator ledger. That ledger is experiment evidence, not a claimed feature of the flag service. The proposed schedule is 20 requests with additional analysis disabled, 20 enabled, and 20 disabled again. Delay one enabled loop until after the final change. Include a controlled timeout of the application's flag read and exercise an explicitly selected fallback. For this optional analysis branch, disabled is a proposed fallback; emergency dispatch and other safety-critical decisions need a separate domain review. These 60 runs are a functional rehearsal, not a throughput benchmark. Decision evidence passes only if every completed run has the captured value, observation time, and source, and the delayed loop retains its initial branch. Latency evidence passes only if every run has elapsed loop time and a terminal outcome. Report percentiles separately for the two branches. Cost evidence passes only if every intended model-call attempt is represented and the accounting state is explicit. Unknown cost must stay unknown rather than becoming zero. Set the thresholds before starting. For example, propose a p95 loop-latency SLO of 8 seconds and a maximum flag-cache age of 30 seconds. Those are test inputs, not measured performance or product guarantees. Report cost coverage beside the accumulated amount: a partial total without a coverage indicator invites a confident but incorrect conclusion, especially when retried model calls are missing from the ledger. A flag write cannot supply model-call cost evidence. Capacity planning belongs in this rehearsal. With one poller per instance, 40 application instances polling every 30 seconds imply about 1.33 flag reads per second before retries and deployment bursts. This is hypothetical arithmetic, not a vendor capacity claim. Add jitter, define maximum cache age, and test the resulting control delay against the actual operational decision. The agent's latency SLO and the flag's freshness budget answer different questions. Buy or build around the incident question LaunchDarkly, Unleash, and Flagsmith are real flag-platform candidates, but a feature checklist cannot demonstrate that the selected integration preserves the evidence this application needs. Run the same rehearsal for each. The table describes selection boundaries and required demonstrations; it does not claim that every deployment passes every requirement. Candidate Buy-versus-build decision Required demonstration LaunchDarkly Evaluate a specialist flag service instead of building flag administration Show decision behavior and change evidence for the selected integration Unleash Evaluate a dedicated flag platform against deployment and operating constraints Establish who owns upgrades, availability, and on-call response in the chosen setup Flagsmith Evaluate another dedicated flag platform with the same synthetic workload Demonstrate fallback behavior, freshness, and incident evidence Infrai Buy a REST flag boundary; build the application evidence ledger Show that polling meets the freshness budget and every run has evidence Custom REST store Build the control contract and operating procedures Own authorization, concurrent updates, recovery testing, and evidence retention Scope Infrai to a polling flag store in this design. Keep application decisions and operator changes in the incident ledger; current flag state cannot replace change history. If the requirement is service-provided change audit, evaluation statistics, parent-child dependencies, or recovery of deleted flags, choose a specialist that demonstrates those requirements. A small REST store is a reasonable boundary only when the team accepts ownership of the surrounding evidence. The trade-off is explicit: Infrai is not suitable as the sole system for audited flag governance. A specialist is the better choice when that is the acceptance criterion. There is an operating benefit when the experiment also uses its model-call surface: Infrai provides 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, with one bill for the platform. The flag adapter and model-call leg therefore need not introduce separate credentials or separate vendor invoice reconciliation.

articles.content: Someone opened your live site, pressed Ctrl+U or F12, and found your Supabase key sitting in the code. Or a scanner flagged it, or the AI that built the app warned you about it after the fact. Now you do not know whether you have shipped something harmless or handed over your whole database. Both are possible, and the difference is one word inside the key. This note is the check, and the fix if the answer is the bad one. The check, in about a minute Step 1. Find the key. Open your live site, press F12, go to the Sources or Debugger tab, and search the files for supabase . Or on your own machine, build the app and search the output folder: npm run build grep -ro "eyJ[A-Za-z0-9_-]*" dist/ | head grep -ro "sb_[a-z]*_[A-Za-z0-9]*" dist/ | head Use build instead of dist if that is what your framework writes to. Both commands are read-only. Step 2. Read what the key says it is. A Supabase key that starts with eyJ is a JWT, and its middle section is plain text that anyone can read. Paste the key into this, in a terminal: echo "<paste the key here>" | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d You get something like this back: { "iss" : "supabase" , "ref" : "yourprojectref" , "role" : "anon" , "iat" : 1762000000 , "exp" : 2077560000 } The word after "role" is the only thing that matters. There are two answers: What you find What it means "role":"anon" , or a key starting sb_publishable_ Not a leak. This key is meant to be public. Jump to If it says anon . "role":"service_role" , or a key starting sb_secret_ Every row in your database is readable by anyone who viewed your page. Jump to If it says service_role . I tested that decode step on keys shaped exactly like Supabase's own, using nothing but cut and base64 , and it returns the role for both kinds. You do not need a tool or a website for it, and you should not paste a key into one. If it says anon or sb_publishable You have not leaked anything. Supabase's own documentation lists a web page as a place a publishable key belongs, because it is "safe to expose online: web page, mobile or desktop app, GitHub actions, CLIs, source code". But read the next sentence carefully, because this is where vibe-coded apps actually get hurt. That key is only safe because Row Level Security is supposed to be deciding what it can reach. Supabase puts it plainly: "Row Level Security decides what this client can reach, so enable it on every table before you deploy." So the real question is not your key. It is whether RLS is on. Open your Supabase dashboard, go to Table Editor , and look at every table. Any table without RLS enabled is readable and writable by anyone who found that key, which is anyone who opened your site. Two of the free notes here cover what happens next, because switching RLS on is where most people's app breaks: Saving data starts failing with "new row violates row-level security policy" "infinite recursion detected in policy for relation", once you add sharing or roles Your project's dashboard also has a Security Advisor page, which checks for exactly this class of problem. Read each finding before dismissing it. If it says service_role or sb_secret Treat this as live, not theoretical. Supabase's documentation is unambiguous: a secret key "bypasses every Row Level Security policy you have. Never put one in a browser, a shipped application, or source control." I confirmed what that means on a real PostgreSQL 16.15 server rather than taking it from the docs. With RLS switched on and a policy restricting rows to their owner, a role subject to RLS returned 0 rows . A role with the BYPASSRLS attribute, which is what service_role has, returned every row in the table, including other users' data , with the same query and the same policy in place. Policies are not weakened by that key. They are skipped. Do these three things, in this order. 1. Rotate the key first. Not last. Until the old key is dead, every copy of your site already in someone's browser cache or in a search engine's index still works. Supabase has a procedure for this: Rotate a leaked or compromised API key . Do this before you touch your code, because fixing the code does not invalidate anything. 2. Take it out of the client build. In almost every case the key is in the bundle for one reason: the variable name has your bundler's public prefix on it. That prefix is not a convention, it is an instruction to publish. I tested this on Vite 8.3.8, which is the build tool behind Lovable, Bolt and v0 apps. I put four variables in .env , each with a different recognisable value, and built the app: Variable in .env Ends up in the shipped JavaScript? VITE_SUPABASE_URL Yes VITE_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY Yes VITE_SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY Yes SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY No Every VITE_ variable was written into the output file as a literal string, the service role key included. The bundler does not know or care that one of them is a secret. The variable without the prefix was not in the output at all: Vite compiled the read of it down to undefined , so the code that wanted it fails loudly instead of leaking quietly. So the fix is to rename the variable so it loses the prefix, and move the code that uses it off the browser. Supabase's docs give the same rule as a comment in their example .env : "Server-only. Never prefix these, or your bundler will ship the key." This will break whatever was using it, and that is the point.

articles.title: Your Supabase key is in your deployed JavaScript. One of them is fine, one is an emergency
articles.headline: Supabase keys exposed in deployed JavaScript: RLS status determines risk level
articles.summary: A Supabase key embedded in deployed JavaScript can be accessed by anyone viewing source code. The key type (eyJ JWT or sb_secret_) and whether Row Level Security is enabled on database tables determine if data is exposed. If RLS is disabled, the key grants full database access. The recommended fix involves rotating the key, removing it from client builds by renaming variables to exclude bundler prefixes, and verifying the key is completely absent from the output bundle.

articles.content: Release: datasette-llm 0.1a11 datasette-llm is the intermediate plugin for Datasette that supports configuring LLMs for use with other Datasette plugins. This release adds support for OpenAI-compatible endpoints, so you can configure Datasette to use an LLM hosted anywhere that talks the OpenAI pseudo-standard web protocol. This means that if you're running local models with LM Studio or Ollama or llama.cpp (which just hit v1.0.0 ) you can run Datasette via uvx like this: wget https://datasette.io/content.db uvx --with datasette-agent datasette \ --root --secret 1 \ -s plugins.datasette-llm.default_model ' { "model": "lmstudio-qwen", "model_name": "qwen/qwen3.8-27b", "api_base": "http://localhost:1234/v1" } ' content.db And you'll get a local server running a Datasette Agent instance powered by your local model!

articles.headline: Datasette Vega plugin updated after 8-year gap for Datasette Lite compatibility
articles.summary: The Datasette Vega-Lite plugin, last updated in July 2018, has been released in version 0.7. The update ensures compatibility with the latest Datasette alphas and leverages new Datasette Lite capabilities to run JavaScript plugins. This enables chart rendering against table data or custom queries, with the README live demo now linking to a Datasette Lite demonstration. The release was made to address long-standing compatibility issues and improve functionality within the Datasette ecosystem.

articles.content: Welcome back to This Week in Stratechery! As a reminder, each week, every Friday, we’re sending out this overview of content in the Stratechery bundle; highlighted links are free for everyone . Additionally, you have complete control over what we send to you. If you don’t want to receive This Week in Stratechery emails (there is no podcast), please uncheck the box in your delivery settings . On that note, here were a few of our favorites this week. The Shocking Demise of Jensen Huang. This week’s coverage was dominated, unsurprisingly, by the shocking and sudden end of Jensen Huang’s 32 year tenure as CEO of Nvidia. The end came on Thursday morning, and just a few hours later, we recorded a Sharp Tech episode recounting Huang’s legendary history, figuring out what happened, and looked forward to what this might mean for Nvidia, the tech industry, and America going forward. Also see Andrew’s view from DC, Jensen Huang Was Always Going to Lose , and listen to Wednesday’s episode of Sharp China about the geopolitical angle, and Thursday’s Dithering about both the parallels and differences between Steve Jobs and Apple. — Ben Thompson Enterprise, Consumer and Intel. The more things change, the more they stay the same: Intel remains on the back foot in the AI era, and the foundry dreams continue to flounder. On the heels of disappointing earnings and 2027 guidance that promises yet more letdowns, Ben’s Update on Wednesday examined the state of America’s would-be national champion by drawing comparisons to AMD, an Intel peer that’s red-hot right now. To understand why one company is capitalizing on skyrocketing enterprise demand while the other confronts flatlining consumer sales, the answer starts with chips chiplets and leads to more profound questions about culture, Intel’s nature, and its bifurcated strategy for the long-term (and, for subscribers, look forward to more on this topic in Sunday’s Sharp Tech mailbag episode). — Andrew Sharp And Then There’s Professional Basketball. As a palate cleanser after a week of Jensen drama, this week’s Greatest of All Talk was a look at the top and bottom of the NBA after the first three weeks. On the euphoric side of the ledger we have Warriors fans (pre-Steph injury), Lakers fans, Spurs fans, and on the other end spectrum there is nothing positive to say in Brooklyn, a familiar malaise in Cleveland, and precisely one silver lining in Salt Lake City. All of it was a great time; we also hit Adam’s experience with the NBA in Mexico City last weekend, the hardest working players in NBA history, and an anxiety-inducing conversation about the number one pick, AJ Dybantsa. — AS Presented by Agentic commerce purchases with Link, Stripe’s digital wallet that works surprisingly well for agents, grew 38x in September. The catalyst was consumer agents like Muse and Instinct. Filling out a web form is not a value-add activity for anyone. No one chooses to fill out web forms in their spare time. That’s why these agents have been particularly useful. I’ve written about how these platforms are giving ordinary people an AI agent with a computer, enabling agents to do genuinely useful things on our behalf. When one of those things is spending money, it needs a wallet that knows what it is, and isn’t, allowed to do. Stripe has learned that’s really about deciding how much freedom to give it. You might approve one purchase, or give it $500 for flights this week, and let it figure out the rest. The wallet’s job is to keep it within those lines while handling everything between “go buy this” and the purchase actually happening. That’s what Stripe is building with Link: You approve what it spends, it can come back to you if the final price changes, and eligible purchases can even come with protection if the agent makes a mistake. You can use Link on Muse, Instinct, as well as many other of the agents you might use already. Stratechery Articles and Updates Jensen Huang’s Affair, The Culper Report, Huang’s Righteousness — Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with a Chinese spy, and that might not be the end of his troubles. I hope he survives, but his influence will never be the same. The Jensen Huang Story Gets Worse, Washington vs. New York, Silicon Valley — The Jensen Huang story got worse for him on Monday; the real risk for Huang is governance, even more than national security. Who benefits? Intel Earnings, AMD Earnings, Intel and AMD’s Divergence — Intel and AMD’s diverging earnings point to fundamental historical differences, and make me wonder if Intel needs to find a new (old) path. An Interview With Roblox CEO David Baszucki About Aggregating Play — An interview with Roblox CEO David Baszucki about how AI is transforming game creation, and why that opens up huge opportunities to both enable developers and make Roblox both an Aggregator and a platform. Sharp Text by Andrew Sharp Jensen Huang Was Always Going to Lose — Jensen Huang spent four years substituting his own judgment for that of the U.S. government. His downfall was inevitable, and probably isn’t over. Dithering with Ben Thompson and Daring Fireball’s John Gruber The Jensen Huang Affair Jensen Fired Asianometry with Jon Yu How Cisco Got Bullwhipped Indonesia’s Mega Rice Failure Sharp China with Andrew Sharp and Sinocism’s Bill Bishop Jensen Huang Likely Out at Nvidia; The Megaspeed Maelstrom in D.C.; APEC in Seven Days; Legislation That May Come Next Greatest of All Talk Agony and Ecstasy After Three Weeks, The “Earn Their Ice” All-Stars, Difficult Conversations About AJ and Season Ticket Holder Decorum Sharp Tech with Andrew Sharp and Ben Thompson Subscriber Mail: Twitter, Microsoft, Bending Spoons, Movie Reviews Nvidia After Jensen Huang, What Huang Meant to the AI Ecosystem, Washington Gets Its Revenge This week’s Stratechery video is on AI on the Ballot .

articles.content: When we use LLMs in a specialized domain, such as the operations of any reasonably-large organization, there is a lot of specialized vocabulary. Such words and specialized meanings will be foreign to an LLM because they aren't in its training set, making it harder for the LLM to be effective when doing tasks in that domain. One technique to aid this is to use an LLM to generate a glossary of the terminology in that domain, and make this glossary available for any LLMs doing work in those circumstances. The sources for the LLM can be any material within the organization concerned such as documents, emails, and chat logs. In some cases getting transcripts of audio or video may be helpful, although most organizations generate enough text to do the job. The glossary-generating LLM should look for single words, and phrases of several words that regularly hang out together to form a meaningful term. The generator should be asked to identify terms that are new to it, but also known terms that are being used in unfamiliar ways. The latter can often cause the most confusion. Once we have a list of specialized vocabulary we can ask the agent to produce a glossary, with definitions for each term. Some terms may be used in different ways, in which case the LLM should provide alternative definitions, with a note as to what context the differences appear in. The LLM can be asked to follow the output format of a dictionary, with a focus on precision and conciseness. Once we have a draft glossary, then human experts in that domain should review it, and amend it for cases where the LLM has got the wrong ends of sticks. We then put the glossary somewhere where any other LLM can use it. It should be in a form that's easy for the LLM to consult, and minimize the tokens the LLM should consume in order to find meaning. We should set up a schedule to review and refresh the glossary at regular intervals, by agents and humans. We should keep it in version control, so we can see how it changes over time. Large organizations often have subtly different definitions in different places, essentially following the Domain Driven Design notion of Bounded Context . Source code can be a particularly interesting bounded context, allowing folks to understand how terminology is used within a code base. Sometimes a single glossary can span several of bounded contexts, but at other times it's better to have separate glossaries for each one, allowing LLMs to consult whichever glossaries that are relevant to what they are doing. I'd urge everyone to resist any temptation to create a single, standard, glossary - I've yet to see that work. Often the value of a glossary isn't to nail down a single definition of a term, but instead to highlight its different usage in different contexts. When there are different bounded contexts it can be interesting to compare different glossaries, or to get LLMs to compare glossaries and describe differences in usage. Comparing a source-code derived glossary to a human text can be particularly instructive. If the glossary is large, it can be worthwhile to only include the terms and links to definitions as part of the initial context. The model can then use the links for only the full definitions it needs while working. A glossary can be used in several ways within Agentic Engineering . Glossaries can inform generation of code, so that names within the generated software fit the particular vocabulary of the enterprise. Sensors in a harness can check for this usage, both in the internals of the software and in the user-interface. When generating code or documents, we may introduce new bounded contexts. For example, internal names that may be used within an organization should not be exposed in a customer-facing UI, because such internal terms are likely to be only confuse a customer. In this case a customer has a different bounded context to the part of the enterprise serving them. It's often useful for glossaries to include terms that should not be used, in which case it includes advice on what other term to use instead. Terms that are deprecated can be handled in this way, with glossary entries that indicate what period of time a term should be in effect. In my conversations with people working with agents in large organizations, a common theme is the difficulty of specialized language. This encourages the activities of domain modeling, building ontologies, and constructing explicit context layers in enterprise data . Getting LLMs to generate a glossary is a simple, but useful, part of this work. Acknowledgements Eric Nagler and Unmesh Joshi related their experiences doing this activity and thus inspired this post. Amy Pellegrini, Annie Luxton, Arun Srinivasan, Chris Ford, Daniel Terhorst-North, Dave Farley, Eric Nagler, James Shore, Jason Yip, Jimmy Nilsson, Matteo Vaccari, Michaël Le Barbier, Pete Hodgson, Pramod Sadalage, Ravi Vats, Unmesh Joshi, and Valentyn Logvynskyi commented on drafts.

articles.title: Bliki: Generated Glossary
articles.headline: LLMs generate specialized glossaries for enterprise domains
articles.summary: When using LLMs in large organizations, specialized vocabulary foreign to the model can hinder effectiveness. The technique involves using an LLM to generate a glossary from organizational documents, emails, and chat logs, identifying terms new to the model and known terms used unfamiliar ways. Human experts review and amend the draft, which is then version-controlled and refreshed regularly. The glossary helps LLMs navigate bounded contexts, avoid exposing internal terms in customer-facing UI, and improve code generation and sensor checks within enterprise software.

articles.content: Release: datasette-leaflet 0.3 OpenStreetMap have a very reasonable policy that hits to their hosted tile server should send a referrer header . Datasette table pages used the Referrer-Policy: no-referrer HTTP header, causing plugins that loaded tiles from OpenStreetMap to violate that policy. datasette-leaflet is the plugin that loads a bundled Leaflet so other Datasette plugins can depend on it. It now sets the referrer policy on the tile requests themselves to strict-origin-when-cross-origin , passing the host but not the full path to the page.

articles.title: datasette-leaflet 0.3
articles.headline: Datasette-leaflet plugin fixes OpenStreetMap referrer policy
articles.summary: Datasette table pages used a no-referrer HTTP header, causing the datasette-leaflet plugin to violate OpenStreetMap's tile server policy. The plugin now sets referrer policy to strict-origin-when-cross-origin on tile requests, passing only the host rather than the full page path. The fix ensures compliance with OpenStreetMap's requirements.

articles.content: Automated testing in the age of AI coding assistants is problematic: when AI agents write both production and test code, developers risk losing the assurance that automated tests protect against functional errors. Matteo Vaccari makes three claims: (1) when AI writes the code, developers become its customers; (2) therefore customer tests, not developer tests, become the primary contract between humans and AI; (3) moving that contract into test data rather than test code makes it easier to protect it from unexpected modifications by coding agents. All of this optimizes for human-readable tests that establish a contract between humans and AI. While in the past DSL parsers and custom test runners were expensive to write and maintain, now AI makes them cheap. more…
articles.excerpt: Automated testing in the age of AI coding assistants is problematic: when AI agents write both production and test code, developers risk losing the assurance that automated tests protect against functional errors.
articles.title: Tests as data: ensuring AI-generated code does what we want
articles.headline: AI coding agents generate tests developers can't trust
articles.summary: When AI writes both production and test code, developers lose confidence in automated tests. Interviews with 26 developers reveal they stop trusting tests as AI refactors both code and tests. AI-generated tests often use heavy mocks that break on harmless refactoring, proving implementation details rather than correct behavior. Moving tests to data files, rather than code, makes them easier to protect from unexpected AI modifications while remaining human-readable. This approach optimizes for a contract between humans and AI, ensuring tests specify correct behavior rather than confirming buggy implementation.

articles.content: Listen to this post: Good morning, This week’s Stratechery Interview is with Roblox CEO David Baszucki . I’ve interviewed Baszucki twice, in February 2022 , and November 2023 . What struck me about this interview is just how much AI has changed the landscape for Roblox. This was a company predicated on the concept that anyone can make a game, but now, for the first time, literally anyone can make a game. That means a world of abundance, and in that world, there is an opportunity to be an Aggregator, and Roblox is aggressively pursuing that opportunity. To that end, we discuss how AI has changed Baszucki’s view of what is possible, what goes into a game creation harness, making games on your phone, and the power of recommendation. Then we talk about Roblox’s vision of a universal player, where a Roblox game works everywhere, and Roblox Everywhere, where Roblox developers can use the platform beyond the Roblox app. We also touch on advertising — the natural Aggregator business model — and whether Baszucki still thinks he is building the metaverse. As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player. On to the Interview: An Interview With Roblox CEO David Baszucki About Aggregating Play This interview is lightly edited for clarity. Topics: The AI Impact | A Game Creation Harness | Roblox Build | Roblox Discovery | Universal Player | Roblox Everywhere | Advertising | Metaverses The AI Impact David Baszucki, welcome back to Stratechery. DB: Thank you, Ben, for having me back. It’s great to be here. So this is the third time I’ve interviewed you, and I want to sort of put that in an interesting context. First, you started Roblox in 2004, you went public in 2021, you first talked to me in 2022 and again in 2023 , that’s like a nearly 20-year stretch. Now it’s 2026, and here’s my question: Is the world more different for you now, compared to three years before, than it was for the entire first two decades from starting the company to the last time we talked? DB: The changes in the world we all feel are sure happening a lot more rapidly. When we first published Roblox — I don’t know if people on this podcast remember — software used to be distributed on floppy disks and CDs. You know, the funny thing is, you’re the second person I’ve interviewed in the last two or three weeks where we’ve referenced back to fact that the reason we say packaged software is it used to actually be packaged! DB: It’s been crazy, we had the Internet, when we started the company, we had the vision of a category called immersive co-experience, sci-fi writers have been writing about the holodeck forever, and we went along our way. I’m still pro-metaverse, we can use the word metaverse, it’s okay. DB: Okay, good, we use them all. It’s Snow Crash — metaverse, holodeck, they’re all good. We started on this vision of building human co-experience, we saw the mobile age come across us, we saw the crypto age. The AI acceleration wave we’re in is faster and bigger and crazier than anything I’ve ever seen, it’s changing how we think about the product, it’s changing how people are going to create games. What’s really exciting is, when we started the company, we had this slogan called “You Make the Game”. Yep. DB: We started with that slogan, we learned along the way that the ratio of people who might want to play games to make games has drifted — more people want to just play games than make games, because historically making games has been Roblox Studio and 3D editing and writing script. We could be approaching the time where “You Make the Game” really comes true, and where making a game is accessible to everyone. It’s really fun, I’ll tell you a bit about some of the experiments we’ve been having with Roblox Build . But we’re entering an era where making a game could be as big as playing a game. I’m right there with you. We’re obviously going to touch on all those points, I think it’s probably predictable what we want to talk about. But to go back to 2023, you called AI then, “a super paintbrush and a super 3D modeler, rather than a full replacement” — Is that still how you’re thinking about AI? DB: It’s what the data is proving out. We just had our earnings call a few weeks ago , we highlighted a lot of acceleration. One, there’s various ways humans can augment with AI on Roblox, they can use MCP , which is like plugging in a model, they can use the Roblox AI assistant to help build. And what do you mean with that MCP server? You mentioned you had 5x growth quarter-over-quarter. That’s where you’re actually using Claude Code or Codex or whatever to work with Roblox? DB: People are plugging in, we can see all of them — Claude Code, Codex, other models — all being plugged into Roblox Studio to help build things. We’ve seen two games hit the top 20 made by AI, we have other metrics like the number of assets. What do you mean by “made by AI”? Because you also said 80% of games in the top 100 have AI-contributed content. DB: Touched by AI, vibe-coded directly with AI, and we can see the count of assets accelerating. Got it. DB: It’s turned out to be, I believe, somewhat faithful to what I said. This is a human paintbrush accelerator, good ideas are still very important, novel types of gameplay are very important. But people are able to flex their creativity much more quickly.

articles.headline: Roblox CEO says AI enables anyone to make games, targets aggregation
articles.summary: Roblox CEO David Baszucki says AI has made game creation accessible to everyone for the first time, citing 5x quarter-over-quarter growth in AI-assisted development and 80% of top-100 games now containing AI-contributed content. The company is pursuing an aggregation business model through AI-powered tools like Roblox Build, aiming to make game creation as common as gameplay while supporting a universal player experience across devices.

articles.content: Before we start, I’d like to share some exciting news: The Pragmatic Summit is returning! It’s a one-day event on 10 February in San Francisco, almost exactly one year after the first Summit. I’ll be hosting and the first few speakers are confirmed. Some faces may be familiar to regular readers and listeners! My goal with the Summit is to make it the single best event for connecting with like-minded engineering leaders and engineers, and curious, driven people. Feedback from last year was that it was the attendees and the quality of debate that made it a standout event. We aim to deliver the same this time with the organizing team, including space for roundtable discussions, and talking with speakers who can stay around after their talk. The Pragmatic Engineer team shall be there too. Applications are open : this summit is for senior+ engineers and engineering leaders who are shaping how modern engineering teams build software, ship products, and scale up to meet challenging demand curves. Tickets are priced at $1,000. You can check out last year’s talks , or watch a one-minute video summary. This year’s Summit is made possible by friends at WorkOS , which is helping organize the event and is the exclusive sponsor. Thank you! I hope to see many of you there! Now, onto today’s article. Sean Allen is a software engineer with deep expertise in building large distributed systems, stream processing, and confidential computing. He is a core contributor to the programming language Pony , which is designed for concurrency. Sean is a distinguished engineer at Antithesis. I was keen to talk with Sean due to his work on confidential computing at Microsoft, as well as his extensive work on the Pony language, and his passion for software correctness, which he works on fulltime at Antithesis. For this conversation, we set ourselves the challenge of discussing modern software engineering without using the phrase “AI” a single time. Read on to see if it’s possible in 2026… In this article, the questions are posed by me in bold font, with Sean’s words in normal font. Today we cover: Software correctness & languages built for correctness. Why languages in the Meta Language (ML) family that are built around strong type systems catch more errors during compilation time than those in the Algorithmic Language (ALGOL) family. Does anybody care about testing? For someone passionate about correctness, Sean is surprisingly anti-testing. He argues that manual testing is the worst way to ensure correctness because you want illegal states to be prohibited from being expressed in a language – even before testing. Workloads & correctness. A more robust way of testing stuff than things like unit tests, is to define “workloads” that can be executed numerous times during a test. A common workload example is The Bank Test to stress test database isolation guarantees. Is quality a “gate” or not? It’s tempting to think of quality checks as closed gates that keep out poor quality. Sean pushes back against this; he says it’s important to consider quality from the very start, and to build with validation techniques that provide feedback on correctness. He prefers this to adding CI/CD quality “gates” late in the development process. Tech debt only hurts if you have to pay it back. Stop being afraid of tech debt because you often don’t need to pay it back at all! Sean says it’s common that tech debt is disregarded during rewrites when a system has become popular. No good fix for supply chain security. Supply chain attacks – when a package gets hijacked by an attacker and malicious code is executed on a machine or service – are very hard to defend against because languages with truly robust defenses, like ‘E’, are unpopular, while popular languages assume a trustworthy ecosystem. There’s no single or simple fix, says Sean. Garbage collection is slow – but doesn’t have to be. A summary of why garbage collection is devastating for runtime performance, and how Sean built a predictably performant approach in the Pony language. Go slow to go fast. Counter-intuitive advice: spend more time designing upfront and aligning everyone, and then you’ll move fast! You can also watch this conversation on YouTube : An amusing detail: Sean and I discovered we share in common a first fulltime employer. We both worked at a company called ‘Sense/Net’ at the start of our careers, although they were totally separate businesses in different countries. The founders of each must’ve been fans of the foundational cyberpunk novel, ‘Neuromancer’ by William Gibson, where the ‘Sense/Net’ name comes from . Note: Antithesis is a podcast sponsor, but this deepdive is not sponsored by them. I’ve just been thinking a lot more about software correctness in the context of AI agents producing more code than ever, thereby creating opportunities for more bugs to ship to prod than ever. I wanted to learn more about this from an engineer with extensive experience in this area. 1. Software correctness & languages built for correctness Gergely: How do you define ‘software correctness’? Sean: “It’s down to whether my program does what I expect. I tend to talk about things in terms of ‘invariants,’ which is a more formal specification term. An invariant is a guarantee that my software does what’s expected of it. But here’s the problem: in lots of cases, people don’t know what they expect their software to do upfront! They know when it’s not working, but they don’t necessarily know what it means for it to be working. ‘Correct’ software does its business purpose and doesn’t wake anybody up at 2 a.m. with an outage. That is correct enough for me.” Your personal definition of ‘beautiful code’ mirrors this. Sean: “I was on the CoRecursive podcast when the subject of beautiful code in Ruby came up. I didn’t really know what people meant when they said ‘beautiful code’.

articles.title: Software correctness & supply chain security, with Sean Allen
articles.headline: Sean Allen discusses software correctness and supply chain security at Antithesis
articles.summary: Sean Allen, a core contributor to the Pony language and distinguished engineer at Antithesis, discusses software correctness, arguing that languages with strong type systems catch more errors at compilation. He critiques manual testing, advocates for defining workloads to stress test systems, and warns that supply chain attacks are difficult to defend against in popular languages. Allen also explains how the Pony language addresses garbage collection performance and advises spending more time on upfront design to reduce technical debt.

articles.content: Google join Jev and OpenAI in the decision model category with "Gemini Decision 1". This new model API is almost identical to Jev: it supports the same three types of questions (yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring) and even reuses Jev's term "Noul" for a yes/no question. It's priced the same as the GPT-6 Luna decision model: 10 cents per million input tokens, and output is free. Jev remains the cheapest of the three, at 4.2 cents per million. Jev is text (and JSON) only. OpenAI can handle text and images. Gemini Decision 1 is fully multi-model: it covers text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. I tested it against video by passing these questions to it along with my Yonkers stomping robot video file: dragon: Does this video have a dragon in it? robot: Does this video have a robot in it? france: Is this video set in France? usa: Is this video set in the USA? Jev and OpenAI both return 1.0 or 0.0 for yes/no questions, but Gemini insists on being a little less confident than that: { "dragon" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.04976021841520312 }, "robot" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.9234055387792485 }, "france" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.08329171353166241 }, "usa" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.9230459995157706 } }
articles.excerpt: Google join Jev and OpenAI in the decision model category with "Gemini Decision 1". This new model API is almost identical to Jev: it supports the same three types of questions (yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring) and even reuses Jev's term "Noul" for a yes/no question.
articles.title: Gemini Decisions API
articles.headline: Google launches Gemini Decision 1 API with multi-model support
articles.summary: Google has entered the decision model category with Gemini Decision 1, supporting text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. Priced at 10 cents per million input tokens with free output, it supports yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring question types. Testing against a robot video showed high confidence for robot and USA detection, while returning lower probabilities for dragon presence and France setting.

articles.content: It’s that time of the year when the November Thoughtworks Technology Radar appears. Again my colleagues have taken a sweep of the technologies that our teams have used in the field, and pulled together a summary of what’s popped up in the last six months. It’s been a busy half-year, one that again has been dominated by AI, and that’s reflected in the many AI blips on the radar. The mass of blips makes it hard to develop a coherent story around trends, but Chris Ford has done a fine job of the writing the accompanying article on macro trends . One team of passionate people experimenting with agents can make almost anything work. They share a context, a credit card and a mental model. They review each other’s work because they sit together, and they know what to check and how much latitude to give the coding agent. Two hundred people, though, cannot work that way. The moment agentic AI becomes an operating model rather than a pilot, a second layer of problems appears: How is context shared between teams? What’s the token bill? How do we deal with increased review demands? What’s the agent allowed to reach, read and change? And who’s now responsible for the harness everyone depends on? Experience so far suggests that the questions that enterprises face are about: shared context, token cost, cognitive load, security, and platform building. While these issues are distinct, they are not separate, so strategies to answer them must take all of them into account. I also echo Chris in reminding us that however impressive these tools are, we must remember that while we have to rethink systems and workflows to utilize these technologies, they should be built to serve humans - and we should all benefit from its bounty. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Ben Thompson’s Stratechery newsletter reflects on the recent election’s impact on data centers . I watch a lot of sports, and particularly this fall, watched a lot of baseball. My Milwaukee Brewers — excuse me, my World Champion Milwaukee Brewers — demanded my full attention, which also meant I saw a lot of campaign ads, and by far the most common topic, at least here in Wisconsin, was data centers. Moreover, it was never entirely clear which way it cut politically: both parties were anti-data center, accusing their opponent of being the opposite. He points out that this opposition is recent, and tied to a shift in focus from the internet and streaming movies to AI: you know, the technology that in the best case scenario is going to take everyone’s jobs, and in the worst case scenario end the human race. There’s going to be a lot said about how Democratic officials will be at the heart of blocking data center building, but as his point above about campaign ads illustrates, the opposition to data centers is (at least at the moment) a bi-partisan opposition. He follows up with “ten takes” from these consequences. The big beneficiaries of this opposition to building data centers will be those who own the data centers that have already been built. The opposition will reduce supply of tokens, meaning that token costs will go up, thus increasing the profits for those who already have their token generators plugged in and humming. There’s also benefits to those who aren’t constrained by the need to build more big data centers. Other countries aren’t affected by a change in US policy, China is the most talked-about case here, but it’s not the only country that may benefit from a drop in US data center building. Apple may also benefit, if it means more AI work is pushed to edge devices that are their territory, in addition to having not sunk so many dollars into AI-specific investments. To his analysis, I’ll add that this may also have a somewhat counter-intuitive effect on regulation, and corporate attitudes to it. The common expectation is that businesses are opposed to government regulation, since that interferes with their free pursuit of profit. That’s true to an extent, but it’s quite common to see established businesses lobby (quietly) in favor of regulation that acts as a barrier to new competitors. So I wouldn’t be at all surprised to see companies that have already built data centers to be pushing for regulations that impede or prevent new ones from being built. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I’ve been a long-time fan of Hadley Wickham, for how he has tamed the rather messy world of R programming into a well-designed tidyverse . He is another thoughtful voice to listen to as we move into the world of agentic engineering , in this case by trying to figure out what the real cost of tokens is . I hear a lot of suspicion that AI tokens are unsustainably priced and that frontier labs are heavily subsidising costs with their VC money. They want to get us hooked now, so they can pull the rug out from under us whenever they want to make a bunch of money. Is that true? My sense is that it’s mostly not. But can I back that up with some data? His conclusion is that it doesn’t seem that token costs are significantly subsidized on per-token API basis, but they are with subscription plans. (He caveats his analysis, saying it doesn’t take into account recouping the costs of training the models.) ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ There’s a creepy excitement at the thought that models are clever enough to edit the weights of models, an activity that Takehi et al refer to as Weight-Space Programming . Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.
